items.title: Anti-coherence Regularized Absolute Scaling for Out-of-Distribution Detection
items.summary: arXiv:2610.32255v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection is recognized as a critical problem in AI safety. SCALE is an effective post-hoc OOD detection method in the activation-shaping family that requires no training data and rescales penultimate activations using a percentile-based magnitude ratio. However, this ratio is ill-defined when negative activations are present, since positive and negative contributions cancel within the underlying sum, causing SCALE to degenerate on backbones such as ViT. We address this with an Absolute Fix that computes the ratio over absolute-valued activations rather than discarding negative activations through ReLU. Building on this corrected scale, we propose Anti-coherence regularization, which penalizes the scaling factor by the fraction of a sample's max-logit contributions to the max logit that are sign-mismatched and thereby suppresses unreliable evidence for the predicted class. Despite requiring no access to training data or training labels, our method ties or outperforms activation-shaping methods that rely on training data in terms of AUROC and FPR@95 on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet under the OpenOOD v1.5 protocol.

items.title: MarineLife-16K: An Attribute-Rich Video-Text Dataset for Motion-Aware Marine Video Understanding
items.summary: arXiv:2610.33478v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Marine video understanding is crucial for a wide range of real-world applications. However, existing marine video datasets suffer from limitations, including the limited number of data samples, fine-grained text descriptions, and detailed visual attributes. To address these limitations, we introduce a large-scale, video-text dataset featuring rich, in-the-wild visual attributes tailored for complex marine environments. Our dataset comprises 2,000 video-text pairs annotated with 13 attributes covering up to four objects per scene, object visual/geometric properties, behaviors, environmental context, and camera motion, spanning diverse lighting conditions, times of day, and 7 countries. From these annotations, we generate 16,080 video-question pairs (12,080 multiple-choice, 4,000 open-ended). Furthermore, we benchmark both proprietary and open-source video-LLM models on video question answering and video captioning tasks. We find that (i) proprietary models often achieves superior performances; (ii) VLMs handle object motion well but struggle with complex camera motion; (iii) closed-source models struggle to perceive camera motion; and (iv) VLMs struggle to reason in static cameras.

items.title: POD-RoPE: Rotary Position Encoding over Physical Observation Distributions for Embodied AI
items.summary: arXiv:2610.33745v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Embodied perception requires positional representations that capture both physical geometry and the spatial and temporal extent of observations. We introduce POD-RoPE (Physical Observation Distribution RoPE), which represents token observation footprints as distributions over camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times. Under independent sampling, expected rotations encode relative relationships between distributions; when each distribution collapses to a single address, the construction recovers pointwise RoPE. The same rotation statistics support Q/K matching and coherence-dependent V/O transformations, allowing observation geometry to guide both information selection and content aggregation. Per-token pre-aggregation avoids increasing sequence length or processing pairs of observation nodes. We evaluate POD-RoPE across four robot policy architectures, simulation and real-world manipulation, and complementary reconstruction, depth-estimation, and novel-view-synthesis tasks. Integrating POD-RoPE into Fast-WAM improves mean success from 91.83% to 92.88% across all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, and from 32.5% to 52.5% on two real-robot tasks on Sharpa North. Controlled reconstruction ablations support the contributions of distribution encoding and V/O transformations. In H20 model-block benchmarks, POD-RoPE achieves median forward-plus-backward speedups of $1.91\times$ over P-RoPE and $5.34\times$ over RayRoPE, with a median latency overhead of 17.4% over Standard RoPE. These results support physical observation distributions as an effective and computationally efficient basis for geometry-aware attention.

items.title: A Sign Law for Entropy Drift under Sampler Mismatch in RLVR
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34044v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), whether entropy rises or falls can depend on choices that matter little under exact sampling, such as whether over-length responses are masked or counted as failures. We trace this to sampler mismatch: rollouts are drawn with top-k/top-p truncation or at a temperature the learner does not apply. We prove that a constant advantage shift then changes the entropy of a softmax policy, at first order and in expectation, with a sign fixed by the sampler. Positive shifts sharpen the policy under any sampler whose likelihood ratio to the policy increases with token probability, including top-k, top-p, min-p, and temperatures below one, and flatten it under flatter samplers. In group-based RLVR with token-level losses, the baseline-dependent part of this drift is set by the token-weighted net advantage, which masking and failing can push to opposite signs. The rest comes from a covariance between advantages and the sampler's sharpness gap and feeds back on itself: in a two-level model, a push away from a sharper sampler takes off in finite time, while a pull toward it saturates. On a 2B model, the entropy slope is linear in shifts of the net advantage under truncated sampling and indistinguishable from flat under exact sampling. Token-level importance ratios leave 98% of the drift, and four clipped minibatch updates per batch amplify it sevenfold. In 100-step runs, a net-zero baseline only delays an entropy explosion, and entropy raised at the start keeps rising only under truncation; cancelling the first-order drift at every step keeps entropy bounded without changing the learner. On a 9B reasoning model forked from an uncorrected run, zeroing the net advantage or renormalizing the learner raises held-out accuracy after ten steps by 8.2 and 8.8 points over the uncorrected rule, with no difference under exact sampling.

items.title: The Price of Scale in Proactive Memory Recall
items.summary: arXiv:2610.34507v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A long-lived assistant that brings up memories without being asked must decide at every turn whether anything in its store is worth an interruption. We show that this decision is a multiple-testing problem whose difficulty grows with the store size N. On streaming replays of LongMemEval, a similarity threshold tuned to 5% false alarms at N=8 reaches 84-100% at N=2048 across embedding models and cue types, and LoCoMo and LLM judges show it too. We prove that a gate which thresholds the best of N independent irrelevant scores at false-alarm rate alpha operates at a per-item false-positive rate of about -ln(1-alpha)/N, which pins its hit rate to the far left of the single-comparison ROC curve and, under regular variation, makes it regularly varying in N. A finite-pool form of this bound predicts the hit rate of a label-tuned threshold on held-out questions to within 6.1 points. At matched false alarms the deployed score recalls 14-26 points more than raw cosine. A cue-swap conformal gate, which ranks the current cue among other cues on the same store, has a finite-sample false-alarm guarantee under exchangeability. With a background drawn from the user's unfiltered history it keeps false alarms at 3-6% on LongMemEval at the hit rate of a label-tuned threshold; on LoCoMo it overshoots or turns conservative depending on where its reference cues come from. In a chronological replay with the user's own earlier messages as references, it speaks on 6-8% of session-opening turns, against 57% for the deployed gate at N=2048, at about 50 ms per decision on one CPU thread. A cross-encoder reranker pays the same price of scale, and on a prospective-memory benchmark, similarity gates recall at most 9% of constraints at controlled false alarms. One human and two LLM annotators judge most false alarms unhelpful for a response. Code and data: https://github.com/RiverChenStillCompiling/price-of-scale

One human and two LLM annotators judge most false alarms unhelpful for a response. Code and data: https://github.com/RiverChenStillCompiling/price-of-scale

items.title: Joint Latent Reasoning and Observation for Agentic Video Understanding
items.summary: arXiv:2610.35229v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Effective video agents must learn not only how to answer, but also where to look next. Transferring this capability to smaller models is challenging because each observation serves two purposes: supporting an answer and guiding the search for further evidence. Textual descriptions may capture what is currently visible while omitting cues needed for subsequent acquisition. We introduce Latent Agentic Reasoning for Video Analysis (LARVA), a framework that distills multi-round video agents through jointly learned latent reasoning and visual observations. Rather than communicating through captions, an observer passes compact continuous representations to a reasoner that selects the next acquisition action or produces the final answer. Crucially, action and answer supervision propagate through this interface, training the observer to communicate information useful for downstream decisions. Observation reconstruction and reasoning-distribution alignment provide auxiliary supervision from textual teacher trajectories. Across five video-understanding benchmarks, LARVA achieves strong performance with 4B and 7B backbones. On VideoHolmes, Video-MME, and LVBench, the 7B model outperforms a textual CoT student trained on the same teacher trajectories by 5.1, 2.5, and 3.7 percentage points, respectively. These results highlight the value of jointly learning how agents represent evidence and act on it when distilling video-understanding capabilities.

items.title: CrowdCC: Jointly Benchmarking Corruption Robustness and Deployment Quantization in Crowd Counting
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36340v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Crowd-counting models deployed on edge devices face two challenges: inputs are degraded along the capture and transmission pipeline, while models are often quantized to satisfy resource constraints of the edge. Yet corruption robustness and deployment quantization are typically evaluated separately. We introduce CrowdCC, a controlled benchmark that jointly evaluates these effects across 23 deployment-motivated corruptions at three severity levels, four crowd-counting datasets, and 26 models. We evaluate TensorRT engines at FP32, FP16, and post-training INT8 precision on an A100 GPU, alongside throughput and energy measurements on corresponding Jetson Orin~NX configurations. The corruptions span six families, with head annotations adjusted when geometry or visibility changes. Our results show that capture-chain corruptions consistently cause the largest degradation across evaluated models, while crowd density affects absolute and relative errors differently. Accuracy on clean images does not reliably predict performance on the corresponding corrupted images. INT8 changes corruption robustness more than FP16, without a consistent direction, and does not consistently improve latency or energy efficiency. INT8 inference efficiency is strongly associated with reformat overhead in the compiled engine, with slowdowns also observed under limited INT8 coverage. Precision changes corrupted-error rankings and robustness--cost frontiers, highlighting the need to consider corruption robustness and deployment cost jointly when selecting models and precision. The code is available at https://github.com/Tulane-Computer-Architecture-Systems/CrowdCC-Release.

items.title: Expert lithological labels do not improve learning when used to predict marine sediment properties
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36410v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Scientific drilling has produced large archives of physical, chemical and magnetic measurements linked to descriptions of the rock recovered. These archives are mostly incomplete: instruments sample at different intervals, recovery is partial, and destructive analyses preclude later measurement of the same material. We train an self-supervised embedding model on the LILY ocean drilling database using six routinely logged properties (bulk density, magnetic susceptibility, natural gamma radiation, and red, green and blue reflectance) across 236,963 observations from 296 boreholes, with a masked variational autoencoder that has a heteroscedastic Gaussian decoder and learnable mask tokens. The embeddings separate geologist-assigned lithologies as well as a variant trained with those labels, and increasing the weight on the labels degrades reconstruction while leaving classification unchanged. The labels are recoverable from the measurements geologists use to assign them, so training on them adds nothing. Lithological categories compress continuous measurements into classes, and compressing them discards what the measurements record about the processes that produced the rock. The embeddings also predict physical properties that were absent from training, on boreholes the model has never seen. While depth should account for this since sediments compact with burial, it does not. On held-out boreholes depth alone reaches a median $R^2$ of -0.02, against 0.20 for the embedding.

items.title: Proposing Better Rollouts for On-Policy Distillation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.36477v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model post-training by letting the student learn from its own sampled trajectories under teacher supervision, aligning the training process with inference-time behavior. However, the rollout policy in OPD is usually treated as fixed: each round samples directly from the current student. We show that this choice can create a compounding teacher--student mismatch, because it requires the teacher to provide effective supervision on whichever trajectories the student samples, including ones less reachable by the teacher itself. On such trajectories, teacher supervision can become noisy or even misleading, leading to undesirable student patterns such as repetition. Moreover, since the updated student in turn defines the rollout policy of subsequent rounds, these patterns persist and potentially amplify over training. This failure mode suggests that improving OPD requires treating the rollout policy itself as an optimization target, rather than only modifying the distillation objective. We propose Mixture Proposal On-Policy Distillation (MPOPD), which derives a student-anchored, teacher-guided rollout distribution from a local trust-region objective based on relative teacher support. The resulting target is a geometric mixture of the student and teacher policies, and we introduce a proposal policy that approximates this mixture, enabling rollout generation in a single forward pass. Experiments on 16 math, knowledge, and medical reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over OPD and recent variants. On math reasoning, our method improves average accuracy by 6.91 over OPD on Qwen3-4B-Base while reducing average generation length by 41%, suggesting that rollout policy design provides an effective way to improve OPD.

items.title: Orthogonal and Parametrized Multi-Attribute Steering of LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37517v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Activation steering offers an effective and efficient way to modify an LLM's behavior at inference time. However, it remains unclear how to apply steering such that the signal is consistently strong and the steering strength has a universally interpretable meaning. We address this first by identifying the most steerable interval for each steering vector and rescaling the steering range accordingly. Building on this, we introduce a more interpretable method for steering, called parameterized steering which instead of pushing activations in a direction, it sets them at the desired trait strength. Next, with multi-trait steering, we find that naively combining vectors causes them to interfere with one another. In response, we develop a method to orthogonalize the vectors; it decouples these traits, allowing a model to exhibit one behavior without inducing the others, thus enabling multiple traits to be steered simultaneously.

items.title: REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37584v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Personalized recommendation depends on learning semantic and collaborative relations among items from online content and user interactions. Generative recommendation (GR) offers a promising paradigm by autoregressively generating discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) of items. However, randomly initialized SID token embeddings and GR models trained from scratch do not directly inherit the semantic relations inherent in items, while inter-item collaborative relations are learned largely implicitly through token-level attention and next-token supervision. To address this limitation, we propose REGER, a unified framework that explicitly incorporates inter-item relations into semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation. We pretrain the GR model through generative semantic retrieval, enabling it to inherit inter-item semantic similarity by learning to generate semantic neighbors' SIDs. We combine global attention with local attention aligned with SID boundaries to capture historical context and directed transitions between adjacent items. We further develop a theoretical framework for hierarchical preference decomposition over the SID prefix tree, proving an exact factorization of collaborative preference distributions and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into prefix-conditional KL divergences. Building on this analysis, we distill a discriminative teacher's full conditional distributions over all legal next tokens at ground-truth prefixes along the target SID path, jointly optimizing this objective with cross-entropy. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over existing GR baselines and support the effectiveness of the proposed preference distillation.

items.title: Behind DeepSeek’s $16 Billion Funding: Chinese Tech Titans and State Players
items.summary:
Chinese AI star DeepSeek’s nearly $16 billion funding round this month involved not only a deluge of capital but a who’s who of Chinese tech investors—and some of the country’s most powerful state-backed institutions, according to details of the round obtained by The Information.

It was only the second fundraising round for DeepSeek. The three-year-old company was the only major AI model developer to eschew external capital until its first fundraising in April. The new round included previous backers—Tencent and battery maker CATL continue to be DeepSeek’s top two investors—but also other tech companies including notably memory chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies and its chairman Zhu Yiming, according to the details provided by two people with direct knowledge of the matter.

items.title: DoorDash and Thrive Go Shopping
items.summary:
Get your deals in while ya still can, folks. And clearly, there are relative bargains to be had. 

DoorDash CEO Tony Xu gets what I’m talking about. On Thursday, Xu finally picked up Instacart, with Xu’s company saying it would pay about $17 billion for the grocery-delivery business. Over on X, Instacart founder Apoorva Mehta sent up a resounding huzzah, saying he and Xu had long discussed such a transaction. That wasn’t news to readers of The Information: We reported on talks between DoorDash and Instacart back in 2021.

At one point in 2021, DoorDash was considering buying Instacart for more than $40 billion. By waiting, Xu obviously saved himself a bunch of money and avoided the ridiculous markups that were attached to pandemic-era darlings like Instacart. Sure, its prospects seemed rosier back then, when we were regarding physical grocery stores as potentially lethal germ pools, but Xu doesn’t seem to be getting a total lemon. In the third quarter, Instacart sales grew 17%, and it generated a decent amount of cash in that time—more than $300 million, a 13% increase. 

The sale to Xu does solve Instacart’s leadership problem: It had looked rather rudderless since Fidji Simo left the CEO role for OpenAI in 2025. Still, Xu will need to figure out how to handle the fierce competition for online grocery sales, a battle that includes Walmart and Amazon (more on the latter company below). 

One thing that held Xu up in 2021 was concern about the Biden administration. According to Valida’s reporting, Xu figured DoorDash wouldn’t get an Instacart acquisition past Biden regulators, who, of course, were trying their hardest to squelch corporate mergers and acquisitions. Those days of dealmaking famine have given way to a time of great feasting: The Trump White House has been, uh, lenient with regulatory approval. It could all shift once again after the midterms. With Democrats seemingly set to retake Congress next week, and President Donald Trump enjoying the same popularity as a DoorDasher who shows up with a carton of broken eggs, the idea of a liberal in the White House after 2028 seems a lot more plausible than it did even a few months ago. 

The prospect of a Democrat in the White House will spur plenty more M&A to happen sooner rather than later. I get it. Judging by the words of liberal standard-bearer Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, the left’s attitude toward mergers does not seem to have changed much since President Joe Biden creaked out of office. On Thursday, Mamdani criticized the DoorDash-Instacart deal, saying in a post on X that such moves often bring higher prices for consumers and “harsher exploitation” for workers. 

In addition to politics, M&A sure seems likely to keep humming for the simple reason that there are plenty of other Instacarts out there—businesses that haven’t fared well since their pandemic glory days. Zoom, Duolingo, Coursera: I could go on. I would’ve put Bumble right there, too, had it not already limped into the welcoming arms of investor Ravi Gupta several weeks ago. (Gupta bought Bumble for about $6 a share; Bumble once traded hands at more than $75.) Other M&A action seems like it’ll be driven by the chance to spruce up an aging business with AI, which I imagine is the motivating force behind the other deal announced on Thursday: Josh Kushner’s $7.6 billion purchase of ADT, maker of home security systems, through the newly formed Thrive Holdings, an offshoot of his Thrive Capital. 

Another reason that I’m going on and on about M&A today is because I listened to what Goldman Sachs’ Kim Posnett, the bank’s global co-head of investment banking, had to say about the topic at our WTF conference earlier this week. By the sounds of things, her direct messages are cluttered with missives from deal-hungry CEOs.

“They’re talking about M&A to drive growth. They’re talking about M&A to help reposition themselves in this new AI landscape. CEOs are leaning in right now—they wanna make big strategic bets,” she said. “We’re optimistic.” Still, as she pointed out, “things change quickly.”—Abram Brown

Amazon’s Agita

If there’s a lesson in the earnings reports from Amazon and Google over the past couple of days, it’s that investors are more in the mood to focus on the companies’ blemishes rather than the strong performance of their cloud units. 

On Thursday, Amazon said revenues from its Amazon Web Services unit had surged 39% to $45.98 billion, its strongest growth rate in nearly four years. That was an impressive feat given that second-quarter AWS revenues grew at a record 37%. And if that wasn’t enough, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy forecast AWS growth rates of over 40% in 2027 and 2028. 

On a call with analysts, Jassy went even further and predicted that AWS could be one of two businesses for Amazon with $1 trillion a year revenue within the next five to 10 years (the other is its stores business—Amazon-speak for its e-commerce business and everything else, excluding AWS).

But, it turns out, that was not enough for investors, many of whom are increasingly on edge about whether tech giants will see a sustainable payoff from the colossal amounts of money they’re spending on AI. Amazon shares dropped more than 6% in after-hours trading. 

The company’s total net sales were $201.9 billion, up 12%, while its net income was $20.7 billion, down slightly from a year earlier, when it had a pre-tax gain of $9.5 billion from its investment in Anthropic. Even though Amazon’s numbers were within its own forecasts, Wall Street analysts were expecting slightly better results. The company left its estimate for its 2026 capital expenditures—most of which is going to its spending on data centers—unchanged at $220 billion.

Google had a similar experience today. Investors punished its stock, sending it down 12%. It appears they were more keen to focus on the bad in its Wednesday earnings report (sluggish revenue growth in its core search advertising business) rather than the good (a doubling of Google Cloud revenues). The AI glass seems to be half full for many investors right now.—Nick Wingfield

In Other News

  • U.S. intelligence agencies found that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese spy.
  • Coinbase’s latest earnings report showed the company had returned to profitability in the third quarter while sales had declined, underscoring how closely tied it remains to cryptocurrencies—despite a push to boost growth through new areas like prediction markets.
  • Intel shares plunged nearly 20% in after-hours trading after the firm said a slump in its business for PC processors would continue.
  • A suspected hack of Binance, a major crypto exchange, could involve billions of dollars.

items.title: Why Private Equity’s Fundraising Divide Is Pushing Newcomers Toward AI
items.summary:
Private equity fundraising has become a story of haves and have-nots, as a prolonged slowdown in firms selling portfolio companies leaves investors with less cash to put into new funds. Giants like Blackstone are still raking in capital while some smaller firms struggle to attract investors, forcing newcomers to find creative ways to stand out. 

Some firms are betting that they can differentiate themselves by pushing AI to transform companies and boost returns. While larger private equity firms are also using AI across portfolio companies, such newcomers are making it central to their investment strategies. 

That includes Aldaron, which has dubbed itself a “transformation equity firm.” The 12-person firm uses an in-house team of engineers to deploy AI at the companies it acquires, though it emphasizes that its goal is to use the technology to grow businesses without cutting jobs. 

In a challenging private equity fundraising environment, “the core message that resonated with people is this transformation equity story,” said Aldaron Partners co-founder Evan Mendez, who previously worked on technology investments at the Carlyle Group. He said the firm has a “hybrid group of investors and engineers that source a company, build the thesis together, cocreate a vision with the management team, underwrite the deal, put their own capital into the deal, and then embed into that company to go execute the road map.”

Aldaron completed its first acquisition in March, buying a majority stake in Oak Point Partners, an investment firm that buys remnant assets like IP and recovery claims. Aldaron funded that deal with money from early investors, some of which also made direct investments in Oak Point. Aldaron continued raising money afterward, closing its first fund in October with $884 million from outside investors and more than $950 million in total including the coinvestments, Mendez said.

The broader fundraising squeeze comes amid a yearslong slump in sales and initial public offerings of private equity–backed companies, leaving many firms with holdings they picked up in the low-interest-rate years of 2020 and 2021. Private equity firms are sitting on nearly 4,600 U.S. companies they’ve owned for at least five years, according to an August PitchBook report, longer than the industry’s typical three- to five-year holding period. That means less cash is returning to the pension funds, endowments and other investors, known as limited partners, leaving them with less money to commit to new funds. 

The biggest private equity firms often have an edge in competing for fresh capital thanks to their long track records, along with their sizable sales teams that allow them to reach various pools of capital including wealthy individual investors. Smaller fund managers, particularly those that are trying to raise their second or third funds after struggling to return money to investors, could be squeezed out entirely. 

“We expect many managers to exit the market, and we are already seeing this as fundraising becomes more challenging,” said Mitchell Mansfield, a managing director at Kroll and global head of fund solutions, which advises fund managers on restructuring and winding down funds. 

To be sure, leaning into AI is just one way smaller private equity firms are finding ways to distinguish themselves. Some are narrowing their focus to a particular sector rather than competing with funds that invest across industries. They can also offer investors more attractive terms, such as opportunities to coinvest in deals, often with lower fees. Fund managers can also put more of their own money into investments. 

Broadwing Capital Management, for instance, started buying companies before completing its first institutional fundraising, betting that an existing portfolio would help win over investors. “It’s a lot easier to talk about an investment with folks than about the theory of a new firm,” said co-founder and managing partner Eliot Kerlin, who launched Broadwing after 15 years at middle-market private equity firm Insight Equity. 

Broadwing, which focuses on manufacturing, industrial services and distribution businesses, launched in 2022 and made its first three acquisitions using money from outside investors and some of the founders’ own capital before hiring a placement agent to raise a larger fund. The firm structured its early investments so they could become part of a growing fund as Broadwing raised more money. The strategy paid off—Broadwing closed its $440 million inaugural fund this August, surpassing its fundraising goal by $90 million. By then it already owned six companies. 

Goldman Sachs Says CEOs Are ‘Leaning In’ on Strategic M&A

Strategic megadeals are dominating the tech mergers and acquisitions landscape right now, Kim Posnett, Goldman Sachs’ global co-head of investment banking, said at The Information’s WTF Summit on Tuesday. That will likely continue, Posnett said, and the bank has a robust pipeline of deal talks across the board.

“They’re talking about really big deals, industry consolidation. They’re talking about M&A to bridge strategic gaps. They’re talking about M&A to drive growth. They’re talking about M&A to help reposition themselves in this new AI landscape,” she said. 

“CEOs are leaning in right now and they want to make big strategic bets,” she said, noting that there’s “a ton of” strategic activity in tech specifically. Posnett’s comments came ahead of DoorDash’s Thursday announcement of a $17 billion deal to buy Instacart. (The Information was first to report last week that Instacart was in sale talks.)

items.title: ‘Skeptical’ Lawyers Highlight Growing Pains of AI Agents
items.summary:
As Anthropic correctly pointed out in its initial public offering filing, business use of AI is in its infancy. Many other corporate executives say it will take some time for white-collar workers, especially those who aren’t software engineers, to use the latest tools effectively.

For example, White & Case, a large global law firm with more than 2,000 lawyers, is “having to hold back” its rollout of one of the newest legal assistants made by AI startup Legora because lawyers are hesitant about using so-called AI agents, said Isabel Parker, the law firm’s chief innovation officer. 

A gradual rollout will ensure lawyers feel confident in using the new agent, which can handle more complex legal work than the AI agent from Legora that lawyers currently use for tasks such as analyzing and summarizing documents and generating ideas, she said. Unlike simpler chatbots, AI agents can take multiple actions on behalf of the user.

Lawyers “are not the kind of people that easily lend themselves to using AI,” she told The Information’s Laura Mandaro during the WTF Summit, a gathering of senior women leaders in tech and finance. They’re “skeptical, they‘re time-poor, they’re risk averse, and they have a very strong conviction that their expertise is very artisanal...This technology comes along and it's a threat to everything they worked for.” 

Legora, a fast-growing app privately valued at roughly $9 billion, aims to automate legal work such as reviewing contracts and drafting documents—the kind of paperwork that needs to be error-free. In an email, Parker said White & Case is investing “significant amounts” in AI tools and that 90% of the firm’s staff uses Legora’s products to some extent. In some cases, using the products can save them as much as 80% of the time it took to manually perform tasks, she said.

Legora’s vice president of engagement, Jillian Burnett, said at the same event that the rapid pace of AI development means that lawyers must constantly learn new tools, which can wear them out.

“We’re working with a very skeptical [lawyer] client base overall, a very busy client base. And when they‘re already having to sit through trainings, different tools...lawyers aren’t necessarily going to want to give you more of their billable time to learn something new,” Burnett told Mandaro at the event.

She said Legora “didn't appreciate that fatigue enough” as a challenge to getting customers to use its tools. Legora has worked to address this by sending its staff to work with lawyers to show how the products can be “hyper-relevant” to their work.

Despite that resistance, Legora seems to be doing all right, and recently said it crossed $200 million in annualized recurring revenue. That implies it generates more than $16 million per month in revenue.

What is forcing change on White & Case lawyers is their clients. Parker said clients routinely ask the firm how it’s using new technologies to speed up work and how it can pass that “value” or new efficiencies to the clients. Now that both White & Case and the in-house legal teams of its clients often use the same AI apps and tools, “there’s nowhere to hide,” she said.

“One thing that cuts through any change fatigue in a lawyer is the client saying, ‘I want this done. Show me how you've been using this [AI tool],’” she said. 

In some cases, though, firms may intentionally slow AI use among junior employees to make sure they learn basic skills. For example, Parker said her firm is considering “sacrificing some efficiency” from AI so its junior lawyers can learn to do their work manually before adopting agents that can automate more difficult tasks such as Legora’s Agent Pro. 

“Most planes are flown by autopilot now...but you need to make sure that whoever's...in the cockpit does know how to fly a plane,” she said.

items.title: Solving for AI’s power problem
items.summary:
The AI race has long been defined by how quickly firms can stand up GPUs. Now, Elon Musk and other leaders say they expect physical bottlenecks, including a shortage of electricity needed to power data centers, to slow down competitors. As utilities warn of multiyear waits for new connections, “speed to power,” or how quickly a data center can get electricity flowing, has become an industry mantra.

The Information editor and writer of The Electric newsletter Steve LeVine moderated a discussion with three leaders pursuing different solutions for smarter architecture, from the grid to the server rack.

  • William Mao, Vice President of Energy Infrastructure, Delta Electronics
  • Allan Schurr, Chief Commercial Officer, ERock
  • Brian Janous, Co-founder, Cloverleaf Infrastructure

The capacity myth

According to Janous, the problem is less about finding gigawatts and more about optimizing them. The grid is underused by about 45% on average, Janous said, because it has to accommodate peaks in usage.

“When a utility says ‘there’s no power for five years,’ what they’re saying is: we don’t have the capacity to meet the coldest winter nights and hottest summer days,” he said, adding that for most hours of the day, there’s enough energy to meet data center needs. (Some notable startups including GridCARE, Emerald AI, Cloverleaf itself as well as Nvidia are trying to figure out how to use such spare capacity.)

Off-grid versus microgrid

Some developers are building their own power plants rather than wait on public utilities’ timelines. But Schurr said going off-grid isn’t necessarily a good long-term solution for data centers.

“It’s a very high-carbon, high-cost commitment,” he said. Instead, he promoted the idea of building a microgrid—a localized power source powered by any number of sources—as a bridge until grid connections arrive. After the data center joins the public grid, the microgrid can still cover peak demand and keep the lights on if the grid goes down.

“It takes three to four years to build a transmission substation,” Schurr said. “We’re building 350 MW microgrid in 16 months.”

Betting on the grid

Cloverleaf looks for sites with spare grid capacity and develops “powered land” around them. Janous said the company has delivered about 7 GW of sites in 18 months, with another 10–12 GW in the pipeline.

Janous agreed with Schurr that going it alone has pitfalls, noting the grid provides services that are hard to replicate, like balancing supply and demand to keep power stable, and restarting the system after a blackout.

“If you have to recreate that behind the meter [in other words, off the public grid,] and think, ‘all I’m doing is building a single power plant,’ you’re in for a rude awakening,” he said.

Simplifying the path to the rack

Mao has watched power infrastructure go from an afterthought to a hot topic.

“For a long time, the electron was not so interesting. Now the space is actually becoming pretty sexy because there’s a lot of demand for the sexy electrons,” he said. That demand puts a spotlight on what happens after power reaches the data center’s door. Delta is tackling that challenge between the grid to the rack.

Mao explained that power typically passes through multiple conversion stages before reaching a server rack. Delta’s solid-state transformers convert medium-voltage AC to the 800-volt DC used by racks in fewer stages, potentially reducing energy losses, as well as reducing the number points of failure.

“Not only do we reduce the number of steps in the distribution chain, but also increase the reliability by removing some of the intermediate power layers,” Mao said.

Solving for AI surges

In the past, data centers traditionally drew steady, predictable power. AI workloads, noted Mao, have changed the game.

“Today with AI, loads no longer measure in kilowatts but in megawatts, and they fluctuate in milliseconds,” he said. Those swings strain the grid.

Managing them takes more sophisticated controls and buffering, he said, adding that Delta’s control platform is built to coordinate different power sources, from the utility grid power, natural gas generation, and to solar and fuel cells. Mao argued that the cleanup should fall to the data center itself, not the utility or its other customers.

Looking ahead, Mao expects the most common setup for large sites to pair natural gas generators with energy storage. Nuclear will play a role too, he said, pointing to a 20-year deal Microsoft signed with Constellation Energy to buy power from a restarted Three Mile Island reactor in Pennsylvania for its data centers.

“You have to have these large blocks of power to move the needle substantially,” he said.

items.title: Encryption Under Siege? OpenAI, Anthropic Disprove Key Cryptography Theorem
items.summary:
Cryptographers who develop encryption technologies may not be sleeping very well these days.

OpenAI and Anthropic both said Monday that their internal AI models had disproven the Exponential Time Hypothesis, a longstanding computer science theorem that predicts the minimum difficulty of solving a certain category of problems. Cryptographers had long assumed the hypothesis was true, and built other findings on the basis of that assumption.

Disproving the Exponential Time Hypothesis won’t endanger any current encryption methods, said Matthew Green, professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University and founder of encryption startup Zeutro. But the finding is a big theoretical step, showing that some problems are easier to solve than cryptographers had thought.

That means cryptographers could also be wrong about other assumptions underlying core encryption methods such as elliptic curve encryption, a method underlying the majority of internet traffic, which would create a scramble to find new ways to keep information on the internet secure.

items.title: Why Publishers Are Adding Invisible Ads for AI Agents
items.summary:
For as long as there have been ads on the internet, marketing has targeted human eyeballs. But as AI agents crowd onto the web, advertisers and publishers are beginning to deliver ads only AI can see, sparking consternation among some of the agents’ developers, who fear marketers could try to sway agents to take actions without their users’ knowledge.

The first publisher to experiment with these types of invisible ads was venerable Time magazine, which continues to generate a significant portion of its revenue from ads on Time.com. Those ads—for Ally Bank and Project Management Institute, a trade group for project managers—first showed up online in August and were developed in a partnership with Mobian, a New York–based ad tech startup. The ads were designed to give agents information about the institute’s expertise in project management and Ally Bank’s online banking services and ATM network.

Following the ads’ debut, Time has had over 30 meetings with brands about doing similar ads for AI agents, and several new advertisers are launching them now, said Time Chief Operating Officer Mark Howard.

items.title: The FlightFinder Occurrence Corpus: harmonising 128 aviation-safety source codes into one deduplicated cross-national accident dataset
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: National aviation-investigation databases are deep but territorial; global compilations such as the Aviation Safety Network and the Bureau of Aircraft Accidents Archives are hand-curated, apply their own inclusion thresholds, and publish no per-record lineage. The FlightFinder Occurrence Corpus harmonizes 279,485 occurrences and 131,882 attached narratives from 128 source codes -- national accident-investigation authorities, occurrence-reporting systems and four global compilations. Records are mapped into one schema; each normalized record reduces to exactly one key from an ordered ladder -- event signature, registration and date, rounded position and date, or source and native identifier -- so a missing field never creates a link, and the key is the occurrence identifier. Records the ladder cannot reach are scored in a blocked pass into an explicit merge table and applied only within an automatically approved score band or after a person confirms them. Field conflicts follow a documented source ranking; one provenance row per contributing source -- its native identifier and URL -- is retained, with attribution and licence terms per source code. Linkage error is measured on five adjudicated samples totalling 200 pairs. A recorded uniform random draw of 60 from the 3,441 merges the automatic band applies as it ships found no error; the exact two-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson upper bound on its false-merge rate is 6.0%, or 205 pairs. The measured error covers the scored band only; the ladder's deterministic joins are not adjudicated. The corpus has no exposure denominators and inherits the under-reporting of its sources. It is offered as a base for cross-national safety statistics, source-disagreement studies and narrative text mining; a frozen, DOI-referenced snapshot accompanies the live API.

items.title: Scoring Explanations Without Reading Them: Structural Shortcuts in Automated-Interpretability Evaluation Data
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37676v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated interpretability scores an explanation of a sparse-autoencoder (SAE) feature by asking a model to predict, token by token, where the feature fires on evaluation examples or to judge whether marked tokens fit it. We find that the evaluation data standard pipelines build can be scored without reading the explanation. On Neuronpedia's stored fuzzing runs for 500 random GPT-2 small features, 91.3% of activating examples are cropped with the peak on the centre token, and a rule that says "yes" when the centre token is marked reaches balanced accuracy 0.979, against 0.838 for the stored LLM scorers (recomputed from the stored per-item verdicts, on marks rebuilt from the pipeline's code); a rule reading only the mark count reaches 0.969. The cue changes form across pipelines: current delphi always marks the same slot in its fuzzing negatives, and full-context runs mark negatives with more tokens. OpenAI's simulation benchmark lists each neuron's top-activating sequences first; a rule that predicts activity on the first five scores 0.227 in pooled correlation against 0.160 for GPT-4's published simulator (post hoc). We give closed forms for what such rules can score; show that one scorer's simulation scores are higher on stored snippets than on natural windows but not shown to be reordered; and build windows that remove the position cue, derive but do not build negatives that remove the mark cues, and separate the sequence cue by decomposition. On natural-text windows cut at random offsets, the best fixed-offset prior shared by all features scores 0.015. On them, that scorer, a typed decision model (Jev), reaches a pooled correlation of 0.331 over 49 features, against 0.013 with shuffled explanations, and an open 8B simulator with the original read-out reads the explanation there (0.194 against 0.019). Scores should be reported beside the best explanation-free rule on the same items.

items.title: The Best Second Opinion Is Right Where the Primary Is Wrong: Partner Selection for Selective Span Tagging
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A span tagger that ranks its outputs by risk can defer the riskiest ones to a person, and a second model can sharpen this ranking. Which second model should it be? Partner selection is conditional, not global: the best second opinion is the model that is right where the primary is wrong. Across eight tagger types, three seeds and three English benchmarks (576 evaluated primary-partner pairings), choosing the partner by held-out accuracy on the primary's errors recovers 82% of the best partner's gain, against 69-70% for span F1 or a random pick. Frozen before a fourth dataset was chosen, the rule replicated there (Spearman 0.40 vs. 0.04 for span F1). Partner value is also directional. The predictive distribution is the second opinion: hard labels discard half of a partner's value, and scoring the served label improves 94% of pairings. Fixed before the fourth dataset was chosen, this score also replicated there. For LoRA-tuned decoders, independently trained partners beat every readout of the primary network. Applied zero-shot to 51 MASSIVE locales, every primary has a helpful trained partner in every locale, and the preferred partner follows competence.

items.title: Exposure Is Not Commitment: Double-Stratified Evaluation of Latent Monitors for Tool-Using Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37679v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool-using language agents are vulnerable to indirect prompt injection, and a growing literature probes model internals to catch unsafe actions before they execute, with sharply conflicting results. We argue much of the conflict is an evaluation artifact, and propose a double-stratification protocol: separate injection exposure from behavioral commitment, in both the evaluation and the training population. On the primary Qwen AgentDojo grid, monitors trained on the naive mixed unsafe-versus-rest contrast mostly learn exposure: they flag exposed trajectories whether or not the agent complies, and barely predict which cases turn unsafe. Retrained on exposed cases only, the same probe families predict the model's own unsafe tool call up to two steps early, the maximum the three-step trajectories admit (logistic AUROC 0.853, matched by a trained TF-IDF text baseline at 0.855). Mistral-7B reaches 0.896 and OLMo-2-7B 0.912; their naive contrasts learn different things: inverted exposure ranking on one, both axes on the other. Representations separate on exposure (probe 1.000 versus trained text 0.908) and where visible context is sanitized or unavailable. Training contrast alone reproduces the shape of recent pre-action-probe negative results, one candidate explanation for the conflict: the signal exists, but the model's own zero-shot forecast and NLA verbalizations do not reliably recover it. An unstratified AUROC overstates what a latent monitor knows, and what a naive contrast learns is population-dependent: evaluations should stratify both.

items.title: Artifact Distillation: Training-Free Transfer from Frontier to Small Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37680v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Closing the gap between frontier and smaller language models is usually approached by distillation: fine-tuning the small model (student) on a frontier model's (teacher) outputs, which binds transfer to training compute and leaves the transferred knowledge largely opaque. We propose Artifact Distillation: a teacher solves training instances and externalizes its problem-solving procedure into an artifact bank that a student queries at inference time, with no gradient updates. Across four LiveBench tasks, a bank written by Claude Opus 4.5 lets Claude Haiku 4.5 outperform unaided Claude Sonnet 4.5 on spatial reasoning (0.707 vs. 0.647) at 60% of its cost, and reach Sonnet 4.5's level on table joining at 89% of its cost. The same raw bank raises Qwen3.5-27B's pooled score from 0.730 to 0.800, showing that transfer is not confined to the teacher's model family.

items.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning for Reasoning Large Language Models: A Survey
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37681v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large reasoning models have recently demonstrated remarkable capabilities in solving complex tasks, where supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on long chain-of-thought data serves as a crucial foundation for eliciting and enhancing their reasoning abilities. Despite rapid progress in both improving and analyzing reasoning-oriented SFT, the field still lacks a systematic survey that consolidates its fast-growing literature. To fill this gap, we present a comprehensive review of recent advancements in reasoning SFT, examining the literature through the dual lenses of methodological design and analytical investigation. First, we review methodological improvements across the SFT pipeline and categorize them into data-centric approaches and algorithm-centric innovations. Second, we reorganize analytical studies along three dimensions: data characteristics, optimization dynamics, and mechanistic insights. Finally, by synthesizing current research focuses and remaining bottlenecks, we outline promising future directions for reasoning SFT. We hope this survey deepens the understanding of reasoning SFT and paves the way for advanced reasoning models.

items.title: Rank-Aware Differentially Private Release of Listwise Preferences for LLM Alignment
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37682v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Listwise preference feedback offers richer supervision for large language model (LLMs) alignment than pairwise comparisons, but a full ranking also reveals more sensitive user preferences. Existing privacy-preserving alignment methods focus mainly on pairwise feedback, while listwise alignment under local differential privacy (LDP) remains unexplored. Extending LDP to this listwise domain raises a critical challenge: the high sensitivity of the full ranking space demands excessive noise, neutralizing the benefits of listwise supervision. To address this challenge, we analyze the interaction between supervision granularity and privacy noise in downstream training, and introduce a rank-aware exponential mechanism that privatizes listwise preference data into a low-sensitivity granularity suitable for downstream alignment. The mechanism leverages ranking information to sample a fixed-size binary partition, concentrating the noise near borderline items instead of perturbing all items uniformly as randomized response (RR) does. Empirical evaluations on downstream LLM alignment tasks show that our mechanism consistently outperforms existing LDP baselines at matched privacy budgets. The code is available at https://github.com/tdsai-lab/RAEM.

items.title: Prompt-agnostic Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Despite their strong performance, large language models remain highly sensitive to prompt formulation. This issue is typically addressed at inference-time through manual prompt optimization, which introduces overhead and lacks scalability. Conversely, we focus on train-time approaches that build prompt robustness into the model during instruction tuning. A common strategy is to mix multiple paraphrases of each prompt into training. We demonstrate that across trainable parameters, the per-paraphrasing gradients interfere, with 57% exhibiting sign conflicts and the naive gradient average discarding approximately a fifth of the magnitude. Therefore, we develop two gradient-merging methods, Prompt-TIES and Prompt-DARE, that address this interference by leveraging interference-resolution operators from model and gradient merging and applying them to prompt gradients. In this study, we compare the efficacy of our methods to increase model robustness to train-time robustness methods spanning all three established classes: data construction, consistency regularization, and contrastive alignment. The evaluation is conducted across four models from two families at two scales. We observe the interaction between prompt phrasing and the specific examples accounts for 54% of per-example variability on average, and exceeds 70% on tasks such as ANLI and WiC. The gradient-merging methods directly improve this local robustness and nearly halve per-example variance on fully fine-tuned models at little cost to overall accuracy. The other train-time methods enhance raw performance, but fail to improve per-example variance reliably. Code: https://github.com/FSadrieh/prompt-agnostic-llms. Model checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/prompt-agnostic-language-models.

items.title: An Introduction to Large Language Models for Scientists and Professionals
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37684v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly become important tools for science, education, medicine, and professional work. Despite their apparent simplicity from the user's perspective, effective and responsible use requires an understanding of how these systems work, what their limitations are, and how their outputs should be evaluated. I wrote this document as a basis for my lecture on LLM in the master in artificial intelligence in medicine at the university of Turin, Italy. This book provides a practical and accessible introduction to LLMs for scientists and professionals. It explains the fundamental ideas behind tokenisation, embeddings, training, inference, context windows, prompting, and instruction hierarchies, while deliberately avoiding mathematical detail. Particular attention is given to the limitations of LLM-generated answers, including hallucinations, uncertainty, reproducibility, bias, and the need for systematic verification and human oversight. The book also discusses privacy, governance, security, and the responsible handling of personal and sensitive information. More advanced topics include Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), retrieval quality, chunking, embeddings, vector search, agents, tools, and workflows. A substantial practical exercise guides the reader through running a local LLM with Ollama and Open WebUI and using it to interact with a collection of scientific papers. The exercise emphasizes evidence retrieval, source verification, uncertainty, disagreement between studies, and the distinction between plausible language and scientifically supported conclusions. No programming knowledge is required.

items.title: From Geometry to Behavior: How Instruction Exposure Unlocks Latent Rhetorical Directions in LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37685v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models do not merely memorize facts; they absorb rhetorical strategies from pretraining data, including the human tendency to reason by analogy. We ask: is this absorbed capability geometrically accessible before any instruction tuning, and what determines whether it can be activated at inference time? We extract an "Analogy Vector" from the residual stream via difference-in-means and show it enables steerable explanation style across seven instruction-tuned models (Gemma-2, Llama-3.1, Qwen-2.5; 2B-32B), improving harmonic mean from 3.22 to 3.94 (+22%) for Gemma-2-9B-IT on 300 held-out test prompts. A small human validation study confirms the LLM judge on Analogy Quality. Our central finding, from seven matched base-instruct pairs, is a gradient of behavioral accessibility: the analogy direction exists in every base model, but its behavioral accessibility under linear intervention scales continuously with instruction exposure during training. Gemma-2 base models (strict pretraining/IT separation) show flat steering landscapes: present but behaviorally inert. Qwen-2.5 base models (instruction data woven into pretraining) are already partially accessible before any explicit fine-tuning; base-instruct cosine similarity of the analogy vector reaches 0.94-0.97 for Qwen versus 0.37-0.66 for Gemma, providing geometric corroboration of the behavioral gradient. This challenges the binary "base vs instruct" framing: the relevant variable is how much instruction exposure a model has received across its full training pipeline. We position activation steering as a complementary interpretability tool that reveals how instruction exposure organizes rhetorical knowledge in activation space.

items.title: One Confidence Threshold, Unequal Coverage: Language Gaps in Typed Decision Interfaces and How Translating Inputs Reduces Them
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deployed classifiers often act on a prediction only when its confidence clears a threshold and pass the rest to a person. We ask whether one threshold serves all languages equally on typed decision interfaces, APIs that return a probability for each option of a fixed multiple-choice question. In a confirmatory study with a written analysis plan, three vendors' interfaces classified 1,000 MASSIVE items, each in 51 languages, with a threshold of 0.9. Even when a request is answered correctly in both English and another language, the English version clears the threshold more often, by 8.6-11.7 percentage points on average. Observed coverage, the share of requests handled automatically, is lower than English's in every other language, while the requests the gate handles are rarely wrong. The gap remains when every language is reweighted to the same accuracy, and a standard calibration metric (ECE) does not detect it on one interface. In exploratory analyses, English's coverage stays higher when each language gets its own threshold fitted to the same 5% error target. Translating inputs into English nearly closes the gap at 0.9 but leaves English ahead at that error target. Requests written natively in African languages show a gap in the same direction when English is their human translation. We recommend reporting per-language coverage at the operating threshold.

items.title: Bouba Beats Kiki, and Other Regularities in the Subjective Preferences of LLMs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Users engage with large language models on tasks that are purely objective ("When was Netflix founded?"), purely subjective ("What should I name my child?") or anywhere in-between. We have rich tools for evaluating model accuracy with respect to objective criteria. However, when it comes to subjective aspects of a task, we do not have similarly developed methodology at hand. In this paper, we take some early steps towards framing the question of subjective evaluation. Rather than measure how often a model is right or wrong on a question, we instead ask, how do models make choices among multiple viable responses without a clear winner? To study this question, we restrict our focus to short-form content, and consider comparison tasks among three such content types: numbers, baby names, and fictional cities. We identify 29 aspects of these short-form examples covering many areas of syntax and semantics (length, alphabetic order, popularity, vowel mix, spoken sound, etc.). We show first that models tend to have strong and reproducible preferences for or against some of these aspects. Second, we show that variations in how the model is asked to express a preference may cause some of these aspects to activate or deactivate in the model's selection. Third, we show that overall preference distributions among pairs may vary radically based on seemingly-unimportant variations in the nature of the question posed to the model, raising new questions about manipulation. And finally, we show that, if models are used both to create lists of alternatives and to rank them, there are unexpected interactions between the two stages that may also drive the models' stated preferences.

items.title: Moment-Guided Optimizers for Noisy Deep Learning: MGO-SC as a Simple Consistency Gate for Adam-Style Updates
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37712v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Adaptive optimizers are widely used in deep learning, yet their behavior can degrade under heavy stochasticity and label noise where the sign and magnitude of gradients can be unstable. We study MGO-SC (Moment-Guided Optimizer with Sign-Consistency), a lightweight modification of Adam-style methods that derives a coordinate-wise consistency gate from the magnitude of a sign exponential moving average (EMA): coordinates whose gradient sign is stable are trusted, while coordinates whose sign fluctuates are down-weighted. We show that the naive form of this gate, which can only shrink updates, loses effective step size and underperforms when the learning rate is matched to the baseline. We therefore introduce a mean-preserving variant that reallocates trust across coordinates without changing the net per-tensor step magnitude. On CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, under a matched learning rate and decoupled weight decay, mean-preserving MGO-SC consistently improves over its AdamW baseline across clean, symmetric, and asymmetric label noise (e.g., +1.4 points at 40% symmetric noise; paired bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero; Wilcoxon p<0.01), while adding no second-order information or per-sample filtering. We report matched-seed effect sizes, nonparametric bootstrap confidence intervals, and paired significance tests, and we release code and raw logs.

items.title: What a Weight Update Buys: Leverage Across Training Stages
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training moves a language model's weights by about a thousandth of their norm and changes its behavior sharply; pretraining moves them by a third and buys a slow drift. We introduce leverage, an exact measure of what a unit of weight change buys: the Fisher quadratic form of an update, computed with one forward-mode pass per direction, divided by the same form for random directions of the same size at the same checkpoint. Leverage orders released Olmo-3, T\"ulu-3, Zephyr, and OLMo-2 checkpoints over four orders of magnitude: pretraining windows sit at the random level on prose, SFT five times above it, RL-Zero and RLVR at 400-1,500, and DPO at 400-23,000. With this instrument we find that pretraining accumulates into noise: windows of 30k to 1M steps are no more consequential on prose than random directions of their size, as a noisy quadratic model of SGD predicts. We find that training precision changes what an update looks like: training bf16 parameters without an fp32 master copy freezes 36-99% of coordinates, lowers leverage up to sevenfold, and creates an alignment between update magnitudes and the diagonal Fisher that fp32 training does not show. We derive and verify a law for reuse: the sign-flip null predicts the relative damage of random drop-and-rescale (DARE) at keep rate $p$ as $(1-p)/(p\,\rho_{\mathrm{sign}})$, within a factor of two of measurement wherever DARE succeeds. Two controls make these readings reliable: every controlled SFT and DPO trajectory with fp32 master weights loses leverage as it moves, and two re-runs of a released DPO stage from its anchor with its published recipe land within 1% of the released displacement and 4% of its leverage, where a plain recipe reads five to six times lower; leaving one component out traces the level to the length-normalized loss and its batch size of 128 together.

items.title: LRMoE: Demand-Side Load Re-Calibration for Efficient MoE Training on Memory-Constrained Nodes
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer scalable capacity for Web applications, but uneven routing creates computation and communication bottlenecks. Existing placement and replication methods redistribute this workload, yet additional expert copies compete with token-related buffers for limited GPU memory. We present LRMoE, a memory-aware MoE training system that jointly recalibrates backward demand and balances the retained workload. During forward execution, it plans retention quotas and expert placement under resource constraints while preserving all routed computations. During backpropagation, a load recalibration metric estimates each token-expert pair's contribution to the expert update and selects pairs within these quotas. A capacity-aware routing algorithm distributes retained pairs among eligible instances of their original experts. Physical compaction then forms smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs, reducing backward traffic, computation, and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B show that LRMoE reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss targets by 21.2-44.8% relative to SYMI.

items.title: Threshold Compatibility and Support-Selection Diagnostics in Neural Discovery of Partial Differential Equations
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37726v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate regression need not yield the correct equation after support selection. For a median/sample-standard-deviation threshold in neural PDE discovery, we derive an exact two-signal retention boundary and a complete-vector perturbation bound. Exact advection-diffusion libraries lose diffusion despite coefficient recovery to numerical precision. True-support refits of forty saved sparse states reduce diffusion error without restoring all derivative accuracy. A fixed sequential threshold ridge comparator recovers exact support in sixty ideal controls but selects extra terms in every learned state. All-fold correct-support candidates are rejected by conditional validation; post hoc energy pooling preserves their higher minimum loss in all sixty states. Supplied-support estimates outperform unchanged selected equations in all 240 physical-residual comparisons on four unused analytic trajectories. With coefficients, observation points and weights fixed, exact replacement of the learned library and target reverses their learned-row ordering in 59/60 states. Weighting both losses also fails the specified Burgers diffusion-benefit criterion at every tested budget. These finite diagnostics distinguish threshold incompatibility, refit damage and score rejection; they establish neither automatic correction nor general recovery or predictive stability.

Exact advection-diffusion libraries lose diffusion despite coefficient recovery to numerical precision. True-support refits of forty saved sparse states reduce diffusion error without restoring all derivative accuracy. A fixed sequential threshold ridge comparator recovers exact support in sixty ideal controls but selects extra terms in every learned state. All-fold correct-support candidates are rejected by conditional validation; post hoc energy pooling preserves their higher minimum loss in all sixty states. Supplied-support estimates outperform unchanged selected equations in all 240 physical-residual comparisons on four unused analytic trajectories. With coefficients, observation points and weights fixed, exact replacement of the learned library and target reverses their learned-row ordering in 59/60 states. Weighting both losses also fails the specified Burgers diffusion-benefit criterion at every tested budget. These finite diagnostics distinguish threshold incompatibility, refit damage and score rejection; they establish neither automatic correction nor general recovery or predictive stability.

items.title: Predicate Neuron: Differentiable Quantization of Predicate Relations in Gradient-based Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37727v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In machine learning, symbolic reasoning approaches often rely on static architectures that hinder integration into deep neural networks and gradient-based optimization. To address this, we introduce the Native Predicate Neuron, a differentiable logic-reasoning neural module that enriches standard architectures with symbolic reasoning capabilities via first-order logic quantization. The proposed neuron models relational logic by learning to alternate between operations using a single trainable parameter. It features a tailored gradient mechanism with a dual-nature formulation: executing hard logical operations during training while maintaining differentiability for backpropagation. By quantizing both its input and choice state, the Predicate Neuron approximates continuous and non-continuous functions, effectively resolving discontinuities that standard deep learning architectures struggle with. We evaluate the Predicate Neuron across Fully-Connected, Convolutional, Recurrent, and Transformer architectures on benchmarks like MNIST and Wikitext. Results show that incorporating Predicate Neurons accelerates convergence, boosts accuracy, and lowers loss in general, with particularly strong improvements in tasks requiring monotonic reasoning or handling discontinuities. Overall, the Predicate Neuron natively integrates into standard neural networks to enable fuzzy logic operations and is available in Keras and PyTorch.

items.title: Amortized Localized Posterior Inference for Model Calibration with Application to an Ocean Turbulence Closure
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model discrepancy may prevent a single calibration parameter from reproducing a physical response across the context domain. In addition, uncertainties in observations and contexts affect calibration and must be accounted for and quantified. We construct a family of localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods according to their proximity to a target context. Gaussian localization weights incorporate context uncertainty through covariance inflation, with reflection at domain boundaries and an optional correction for uneven context sampling. A conditional normalizing flow approximates the family of posteriors through amortized variational inference. Integrating the localized posteriors under a prescribed context measure gives the marginalized parameter distribution. In a twin experiment with the Branin-Hoo model, we compare global and localized inference under uniform and skewed context distributions. Localization reduces the reported aggregate predictive errors relative to the global posterior. An application to the k-$\epsilon$ turbulence closure in a single-column ocean model, with atmospheric surface forcing as context, shows that localized posterior calibration reduces temperature and zonal-velocity errors relative to deterministic and global-posterior calibration. Both twin experiments are constructed to admit local compensation.

items.title: ThinkJev: One Thought, Every Budget for Calibrated Typed Decisions
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. Reading those probabilities from one forward pass is fast but often wrong on decisions that take several steps, such as arithmetic, counting, and date comparison. Letting the model think first fixes most of these errors, but costs seconds per decision instead of milliseconds. To pay for thinking only where it helps, ThinkJev builds a fast and a slow system from one open hybrid-thinking model that can answer directly or after a thought. System 1 reads the model's probabilities for the option letters when it answers directly; System 2 reads the same letters after the model has thought on the same cached prompt, so escalating repeats no work and both systems give probabilities over the same options. Because the letters can be read after any number of thought tokens, one sampled thought also gives the answer under every thinking budget. Without training, ThinkJev lets System 1 answer alone only where a statistical test on labeled dev data guarantees that its accepted answers stay under a target error rate. At a 5% target, Qwen3.5-27B answers 24.5% of 8359 test decisions this way with a realized error of 3.9% (Qwen3.5-4B and 9B: 6.5% and 0.0%). For the rest, stopping each thought as soon as its answer is confident reaches 81.6% accuracy, against 82.7% for always thinking, with 72% of the thought tokens. Choosing when to think from System 1's confidence alone saves less, because the decisions System 1 is least sure of are often not the ones thinking fixes. On the public items of JevBench, an independent benchmark of typed-decision services, Qwen3.5-27B thinks on 29.4% and is not distinguishable in accuracy from the two thinking APIs listed (exploratory). Code and data generators are available at https://github.com/ding-xiaolu/ThinkJev.

items.title: Selective Transfer Learning for Groundwater Level Anomaly Forecasting: Accuracy-Risk Trade-offs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37733v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work studies context-aware selective transfer learning for multi-well groundwater anomaly forecasting in the Netherlands. Source-domain pretraining can raise average accuracy but is not uniformly reliable: it degrades performance on a substantial fraction of heterogeneous wells. Context-Aware Selective Learning (CASL) uses calibration-trained, constrained contextual blending of frozen no-transfer and fixed-transfer parents. Global Convex Blend uses the same parents with one calibration-fitted weight per seed. The corrected task requires nine consecutive observed monthly inputs and an exact three-calendar-month target, without interpolation. Evaluation covers 457 wells and 13,718 test windows under five predefined seeds, with the four-cell maxsim0.60 source pool frozen using Always-TL validation RMSE alone. Fixed transfer harms 18.38-51.86% of wells. CASL has 0.424-1.084% lower RMSE than No TL, partially rescuing 97.53-99.50% and fully rescuing 23.46-43.78% of fixed-harmed wells. Partial rescue can arise structurally from convex blending and does not establish contextual superiority. Global Convex Blend protects more wells in four seeds, while CASL has slightly lower pooled RMSE in four. Neither dominates: the results support an accuracy-risk trade-off on the fixed split, not rolling deployment validity.

items.title: Anisotropic Trust Region Warping for Prior-Data Fitted Networks in Bayesian Optimisation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37737v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) replace the hyperparameter refitting of Gaussian Process (GP) surrogates in Bayesian optimisation with a single forward pass, at the cost of a prior that is fixed at meta-training time. We show empirically that a PFN's predictive log-likelihood falls increasingly behind that of a refitted GP as the objective function's lengthscale grows beyond the mode of the PFN's meta-training prior, and that this deficit carries over to optimisation performance. To correct the mismatch without retraining the network, we introduce Anisotropic Trust Region (ATR) warping. Per-dimension lengthscales are estimated by kernel target alignment, and an affine rescaling of the input space maps the objective onto the lengthscale the PFN expects, with a trust region around the anchor determining which observations are retained, leaving the PFN's $\mathcal{O}(d \cdot N^2)$ inference cost unchanged. On functions drawn from a Mat\'ern-3/2 kernel, ATR warping improves optimisation performance of the PFN at both extremes of the lengthscale range. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/youngers2006/Trust-Region-Warping-For-PFNs.
