items.title: A Low-Rank Space Captures Linear Alignment Between LLM and Human Neural Activity During Naturalistic Language Listening
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40511v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as computational models of human language processing, yet it remains unclear which components of their representations drive alignment with neural activity. Here, we use ridge reduced-rank regression to identify the brain-predictive subspace of LLM representations: the representational directions that support linear prediction of neural responses. Across three naturalistic language-listening datasets spanning intracranial electrophysiology and fMRI, and six model conditions spanning autoregressive, bidirectional masked, and randomly initialized language models, we find that full linear encoding performance can be recovered using only 1-3% of the original embedding dimensionality. These low-dimensional subspaces generalize across held-out participants and, to a lesser extent, across datasets, suggesting that neural predictivity is concentrated in a compact and partially shared representational space. We next compare these brain-predictive directions with the principal axes of variation in the embeddings. Principal component analysis requires substantially more dimensions to recover neural prediction, demonstrating that the directions most useful for predicting neural activity are distinct from those capturing the most overall variance within LLM representations themselves. Finally, characterizing the learned subspaces allows us to surface interpretable features that are overrepresented in neural activity above and beyond the LLM representations. Together, these results show that LLM-brain alignment is supported by a small, structured subset of model representations and provides a framework for better understanding exactly why these representations align. Code can be found at: https://github.com/thefinnlab/low-rank-alignment

items.title: How I Aligned Your Model: Scaling Up Multilingual Safety Training with Templates
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40516v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety alignment for Large Language Models is heavily focused on English with limited multilingual representation, particularly damaging low-resource language performance. Related open training datasets are often limited in size or do not follow region-localized harmful topics to broaden the scope of alignment beyond cultures. We propose a scalable template-based augmentation pipeline to produce massive multilingual refusal and benign corpora, extracting safe templates from harmful prompts, translating them and then filling in the slots with culturally authentic entities, both harmful and benign. As a result, we release MSafeTemp, a validated corpus spanning 60 languages useful for multilingual safety alignment and evaluation. Using the dataset, we show that English-only evaluation misjudges multilingual safety: for several models, attacks that fail in English succeed once translated, while culturally localized variants expose further failures that translation alone misses. We also confirm that augmenting safety training data through templates allows for higher diversity and quality of alignment, resulting in improved safety performance beyond English. MSafeTemp and the respective pipeline are aimed at facilitating research and development of safer and more responsible models for less-represented cultures.

items.title: IndicIPR-QA: A Benchmark for Extractive Question Answering on Indian IPR Laws
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Legal Question Answering (QA) over statutory texts is a challenging task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), especially in low-resource settings with complex legal systems. It requires answers that are precise and grounded in the law. However, to the best of current knowledge, no existing extractive QA benchmark provides exact answer spans from statutory texts across all seven Indian Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) Acts. This paper presents IndicIPR-QA1, an extractive QA benchmark for Indian IPR laws. The proposed dataset contains 4,462 QA pairs from 1,116 statutory contexts across seven Acts. Questions and answers are generated using GPT-4o and validated through nine automatic quality checks, single and multi-model LLM evaluations, and a 200-pair human audit. Section-level partitioning prevents source-context overlap across the training, validation, and test sets. Further analysis examines answer span length, lexical overlap, and multi-clause structure across the corpus and individual Acts. BM25 achieves a token-level F1 score of 20.21, while fine-tuned InLegalBERT reaches 85.02 under a unified sliding-window inference protocol. The large performance gap between BM25 (20.21 F1) and InLegalBERT (85.02 F1) shows that simple word matching is not enough to answer these legal questions. Performance also varies across the seven Acts, indicating substantial differences in answer-extraction performance.

items.title: Homebrewed SLMs: Autoregressive and Masked Diffusion Language Models Built at Home for Portuguese
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building a language model of one's own no longer requires a data centre. This tutorial trains one from scratch, tokenizer included, on one consumer GPU, and shows how to tell whether it is good for the tasks of a specialist domain. It proposes no new method. It releases a tested Python package and two notebooks in Brazilian Portuguese with autoregressive and masked diffusion generation on one network, a preregistered comparison protocol, legal tasks built from text alone with a Kneser-Ney floor and public yardsticks, reference numbers for models of 11 to 12M parameters, and a catalogue of defects that only measurement revealed. On Brazilian prose and federal laws, at minutes per run, the autoregressive mode peaks at 64 epochs over the same text and then memorises it, while masked diffusion improves up to 256. At their best points on test, the diffusion bound exceeds the autoregressive likelihood by 0.06 bits per byte, within the preregistered minimum effect. On held-out laws and on acts published after training, the model ties a 6-gram floor in likelihood on the same windows, and it loses to the floor at continuing those acts. It beats the floor at detecting tampered text, and fills cross-references more often than the floor and public models of 160M and 630M parameters, only in decrees, a genre absent from training, where those scorers stay near or below chance, and in filling the blank only when each group weighs the same, since per item it ties the 630M model. On laws, the public models, trained with about 5x10^2 to 10^5 times its compute, lead in tampered text and continuation. The blind human reading is preregistered and not part of this version.

items.title: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40535v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems. One proposed approach uses relativizing interactive proofs, in which a weak verifier checks the output of a complex oracle-aided computation by interacting with one or more powerful provers. A prominent example is debate, which is highly efficient but assumes that one of two powerful AI models, or provers, is truthful. For certain classes of oracle-aided computations, this assumption can be removed, but at substantially greater computational cost. In this work, we introduce \emph{rewindable interactive proofs} (RIPs), a new model of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight. In an RIP, the verifier may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. This is possible when the prover is an AI model, since the verifier can save a snapshot of the model's state and later restore it. We construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. Our construction is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover, and it uses no cryptography. In our construction the honest prover runs in time linear in that of the original computation, and the verifier, after a one-time preprocessing step, runs in time nearly linear in the input length (which can be much smaller than the computation itself). We implement our protocol, report a preliminary MNIST experiment, and show that an RIP can be faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system. RIPs may be of independent interest. Rewinding is possible whenever the verifier controls the prover's machine, for example when the prover runs on trusted hardware or in a virtual machine whose state can be checkpointed.

items.title: On the Fundamental Limits of Prefill-Based Decoding Length Prediction
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40541v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Predicting how many tokens a large language model (LLM) will decode, using only prefill-phase hidden states, is a key primitive for inference scheduling. We show that current benchmarks conflate predictor quality with task hardness: when the target model, dataset, or sampling configuration changes, reported accuracy collapses even though the predictor is unchanged. We trace this instability to an overlooked error source---the inherent stochasticity of autoregressive decoding---and derive bounds that every prefill-side method must obey. Our analysis treats decoding as a stopped stochastic process. The per-step stopping probability of a response is not constant but ramps up over hundreds of steps, so the decode length inherits a central limit theorem from the many local decisions that determine where a response ends; this yields per-prompt normality with an explicit error term, together with an affine variance law $\sigma=\alpha\mu+b$ whose slope is the coefficient of variation of the number of response segments. Empirically, the normal law reproduces the per-prompt MAE and the central mass of the decode-length distribution to within a few percent, and the residual departures from normality (mild right skew, slight excess kurtosis) are the ones predicted by the sampling-noise correction. Under fixed model, data, and sampling conditions, a broad design space of predictors (MLP, EGTP, FiLM, soft-label, and Mixture-of-Experts variants) converges to similar performance close to the bound, confirming that \emph{system error dominates model error}. We argue for a benchmarking protocol that fixes the model, data, and sampling parameters and that reports relative-error metrics alongside absolute ones. Code and analysis tools are available at https://github.com/ShwStone/DecodingPredict.

items.title: Machine Learning-Based Detection of Mobile Money Scan Messages in Ghana: A Comparative Evaluation of Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, and Randon Forest Classifiers
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40544v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mobile money (MoMo) is Ghana's preferred retail payment channel, recording GHC518.4 billion in transactions in December 2025 and over 26.7 million active accounts (Graphic Online, 2026). This growth has coincided with increased social-engineering fraud over Short Message Service (SMS) and Unstructured Supplementary Service Data (USSD), where fraudsters impersonate network operators, agents, relatives, or regulators to obtain personal identification numbers (PINs), identity data, or funds. We present a supervised machine-learning pipeline for classifying scam and legitimate Ghanaian MoMo SMS messages using a labelled corpus of 220 messages across 18 scam and legitimate subcategories. Domain-specific normalisation of currency amounts, phone numbers, and USSD codes preceded TF-IDF vectorisation of unigrams and bigrams. Using stratified five-fold cross-validation and a 20% held-out test set, we trained and evaluated Multinomial Naive Bayes, linear support vector machine (SVM), and Random Forest classifiers using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC). Held-out accuracy, F1, and AUC were 1.00 for Naive Bayes and linear SVM; cross-validated accuracy averaged 96.6% (+/-3.3), 94.9% (+/-4.6), and 92.0% (+/-4.2). Discriminative n-grams reflected imperative urgency ("send," "claim," "please send") and PIN solicitation ("PIN," "pincode"); legitimate messages featured confirmatory and cautionary language ("balance," "successful," "do not share"). Findings are contextualised in Sub-Saharan African SMS fraud detection, small template-based corpus ceiling effects, and a pathway toward larger naturalistic multilingual corpora. Interpretable classical classifiers achieve high accuracy on structured MoMo scam text and suit carrier- or handset-level filtering in low-resource, on-device settings.

items.title: Retrieval as Traversal: Value-Indexed Memory for Stateful Long-Context Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40545v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-context models repeatedly solve closely related retrieval problems. Attention or global retrieval can retain large stores, but each forward pass again searches for what matters. Recurrent compression avoids this search only by deciding earlier what information to preserve. Neither mechanism directly exploits that useful memories at neighbouring retrieval steps may substantially overlap. We propose an alternative in which retrieval is a persistent local traversal through an address space. We separate a memory's content from its address. Utility is defined by the information revealed by retrieving the content, while geometry determines only how cheaply that information can be reached. This leads to a cost-regularised indexing objective that preserves information value inside local neighbourhoods while charging for every memory made locally accessible. Its marginal-value form gives both attractive and exclusion pressures. Thus, complementary memories should be co-retrievable when the additional value exceeds retrieval cost, whereas redundant memories should not occupy the same retrieval set solely because they are individually useful. As a proof of principle, we test only the simplest fixed-geometry instance on MiniGrid Memory. A persistent local traversal head reaches $0.95$ mean return after $0.59$M training steps with a five-token context, compared with $0.94$M for Gaussian absolute addressing and more than $2$M for categorical absolute addressing. The experiment does not test learned geometry or repeated retrieval. Instead, it motivates the hypothesis that stateful retrieval may be easier to learn than stateless. To test the full proposed method further experimentation is necessary.

items.title: Ramanujan Challenge Results: AI-Assisted Evaluation Pipeline for Multi-Format Proofs
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40551v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI's mathematical capabilities rapidly improve, meaningful benchmarks are shifting from university-level problems and math olympiads to research-level mathematics. The Ramanujan Challenge is a benchmark comprised of research-level problems in number theory, including unpublished results and open conjectures. It presented concrete formulas for mathematical constants whose correctness can be checked numerically, while their proofs may require non-obvious mathematics. Here, we analyze the Challenge submissions, measuring the relative success of different AI models, Computer Algebra Systems (CAS), and formal tools. We find correct submissions that are conceptually distinct from the official solutions, and a proof of one of the published open conjectures. Evaluating the submissions exposed a second challenge: judging complex proofs reliably at scale. We introduce an AI-assisted evaluation pipeline for natural language proofs, CAS code, and Lean formalizations that assesses semantic and logical correctness. Compared with the conventional one-shot LLM judgment, our pipeline reduces false-positive verdicts on natural language proofs from 23% to 6% and improves judgment accuracy on supporting code from 46% to 58%. This approach provides a methodology for evaluating research-level mathematics at scale, with potential applications across mathematics and AI for science.

items.title: Advancing Clinical Genomic Analysis with a Skill-Centred Agent
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40556v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Clinical genomic analysis requires experts to integrate evolving guidelines, databases, and computational evidence. As sequencing has become increasingly accessible, this complex and labor-intensive process has become a major bottleneck to the timely use of genomic information in clinical decision-making. To fill this gap, we developed ClinGeX, a large-language-model agent that composes 105 curated executable skills through task-specific retrieval and dependency-aware orchestration. On 223 temporally held-out benchmark cases, ClinGeX achieved 71.7\% macro-averaged task-level concordance with expert reference classifications, compared with 45.7\% for the strongest comparator. In a three-condition, counterbalanced human-AI collaboration study, 45 clinical genomic professionals assessed 135 clinically derived cases under routine (no AI assistance), DeepSeek-assisted and ClinGeX-assisted conditions. ClinGeX assistance increased raw case-level concordance across criterion-level variant analysis, genomic interpretation in rare disease and molecular oncology decision-making (51.1\%, 57.8\%, 64.4\% versus 15.6\%, 31.1\%, 20.0\% in comparator conditions) and reduced reported interpretation time in all scenarios. During an exploratory one-month real-world non-interventional assessment, 11 experienced professionals submitted feedback on 96 self-selected analysis episodes and reported frequent conclusion adoption and time savings. These findings support executable domain skills as a promising approach to augment specialist genomic interpretation.

items.title: FARMS: A Verifiable Foundation for Automated Computational Science
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40560v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated computational science could accelerate discovery by selecting, adapting and developing numerical methods. This prospect requires mathematical knowledge that AI systems can interpret and reuse with explicit guarantees. Here we present FARMS, a faithful and efficient foundation that transforms computational mathematics into AI-ready computing knowledge. FARMS connects formal statements to source context, algorithmic meaning and quantitative guarantees through source preparation, reusable representations and semantic review. Across 171 targets in randomized numerical linear algebra and numerical partial differential equations, 157 were accepted by the pipeline, with mean estimated costs of US \$0.85-2.29 per target across sources. Lean-checked implications from explicit source premises connect selected statements to computational skills, illustrated by a heat-flow solve and wave-response compression. FARMS therefore supports an affordable, reusable knowledge foundation for trustworthy automated computational science.

items.title: Comparing Human Role-Players and LLM-Simulated Clients in Online Counselling Training: An Analysis of Counselling Patterns
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study investigates the capabilities of Large Language Models to simulate counselling clients in educational role-plays in comparison to human role-players. Initially, we recorded role-playing sessions, where novice counsellors interacted with human peers acting as clients, followed by role-plays between humans and clients simulated by Mistrals Mixtral 8x7b using 4-bit quantization. These interactions were analysed with a counselling communication pattern system at sentence level. We investigated two key questions: (1) to what extent LLM-generated responses replicate authentic conversational dynamics and (2) whether counsellors' communication behaviour differs when interacting with human versus LLM-simulated clients. The findings highlight both similarities and differences in the application of counselling patterns across scenarios, showing the potential of LLM-based role-playing exercises to enhance counselling competencies and to identify areas for further refinement in virtual client simulations.

items.title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.

raw_fields.title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm
raw_fields.summary: arXiv:2610.40564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Foundation models are typically trained in stages: pretraining, midtraining, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and reinforcement learning (RL), with changes in both data and learning algorithms. We show that this algorithmic separation is not fundamental. By deriving suitable RL objectives as maximum-likelihood fitting to model-generated target distributions, we place all of these stages under a single likelihood-based training algorithm, unified training. This perspective turns the foundation-model training lifecycle into a problem of choosing which data to train on, in what proportions, and when, with conventional staged training as a special case. We instantiate this framework in a unified training system that mixes static data and RL generations within a single trainer. Across controlled and real-world experiments, unified training improves the accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage while preserving broader capabilities, and provides a stronger starting point for continual learning. This work lays the groundwork for a unified science of foundation-model training, connecting mathematical principles, training infrastructure, and the development of model capabilities.

items.title: Every Token Needs Its Own Teacher: Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-distillation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40574v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy Self-distillation (OPSD) has proven effective for post-training large language models by constructing a teacher conditioned on privileged references. However, existing approaches keep the teacher fixed either throughout training by consistently exposing it to the full reference, or within each response by adaptively varying partial reference exposure only across responses. In this paper, we argue that neither of them is sufficient. Instead, every token needs its own teacher, as the teacher preference can vary token by token within the same response. Through a teacher-intervention pilot study, we validate that the teacher preference differs across tokens, and reveal that a preferred teacher can be identified for each token through majority voting and KL-based selection. Motivated by these findings, we propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation (MTA-OPSD), the first token-level adaptive OPSD method. Our method constructs a multi-teacher pool consisting of candidate teachers, and enables every token to adaptively select its preferred teacher during training. Experiments with Qwen3 models on mathematical reasoning tasks show that MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD approaches with an average gain of up to $+5.9$ over the base model, highlighting the importance of adapting teacher supervision at the token level. The code is available at https://github.com/xingzhejun/MTA-OPSD.

items.title: PIVOT: Progressive Intervention via Online Teacher Correction
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40576v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) is limited by sparse outcome-level feedback on hard reasoning tasks: when all rollouts in a group fail, rewards provide no learning signal. Stronger teachers can provide additional guidance, but this raises a central question: how can such signals be incorporated into RLVR to support successful rollouts while remaining learnable for the student? We distinguish two complementary mechanisms: trajectory-level intervention, which improves access to reward-bearing trajectories, and token-level supervision, which provides dense targets to guide student learning. Our controlled experiments show that either mechanism alone can remain insufficient, motivating their combination. We therefore introduce PIVOT, which inserts teacher-generated corrections into student rollouts and applies token-level KL supervision to these segments alongside the RLVR objective. Beyond their combination, we systematically analyze where to intervene and how to supervise, yielding a recipe for effective guidance. Across hard logic games and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, PIVOT consistently outperforms existing methods, nearly doubling mean avg@8 on logic games from 19.5% for the best-performing baseline to 35.6%.

items.title: Multi-View MoE: Letting Every Router Shape Expert Computation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40577v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) models expand parameter capacity by activating a small subset of experts per token. Expert selection directly affects model capabilities under a fixed active-expert budget. Dense evaluation of all experts reveals weak agreement between single-router rankings and expert-utility evaluation rankings, especially in middle and deep layers. Richer signals for selection and computation incur additional cost: selection based on internal expert activations requires preliminary computation, while processing multiple full representations separately through the same expert repeats its computation. We propose Multi-View MoE to improve expert selection with multiple routers and reuse their preferences to modulate expert computation under a fixed expert budget. Its Multi-Router submodule aggregates sigmoid scores from independently initialized routers. These routers develop highly differentiated expert preferences during training, allowing experts strongly favored by one router or jointly supported by several routers to be selected. Multi-View further uses each selected expert's relative scores across routers to mix learned latent views into its input, reusing routing preferences for both selection and computation. Each selected expert executes one forward pass, preserving the active-expert count, expert FLOPs, and all-to-all communication volume. On a 24-layer 10B-A1B model trained on 708B tokens, full Multi-View MoE improves the nine-task downstream mean by 1.18 percentage points over the baseline. Multi-Router alone yields a 0.6-percentage-point gain and improves the rank correlation between router scores and evaluated expert utility, with relative increases of 8.1% globally and approximately 58% in the layer with the lowest single-router alignment. Controlled mixing interventions show the model uses input differences that depend on both the expert and the token.

items.title: VeriCUA: Verification as Agentic Exploration for Computer-Using Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40578v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building and scaling computer-using agents (CUAs) across desktop, mobile, and web environments requires reliable task-completion verification for data curation, evaluation, and reinforcement learning. Typical automated approaches prompt vision-language models (VLMs) to judge trajectories or generate programs to inspect application state. However, both rely on partial views of complex digital environments. VLM judges are restricted to supplied observations, while generated programs depend on accessible state. These views can omit decisive evidence or leave completion judgments unsupported. Tailoring separate verifiers to different platforms and access settings adds further engineering cost. We present VeriCUA, a platform-agnostic framework for verification through agentic exploration. It treats verification as dynamic evidence gathering and assessment within a shared procedure for online and offline settings across platforms and observation modalities. After inspecting the available context to construct a task rubric, the verifier selects GUI or code checks for unresolved requirements and combines their findings under explicit evidence rules. Experiments show improved agreement with reference labels over the compared baselines across these settings, with the largest offline gains on hard cases and stronger rejection of false completion claims online. Further analyses connect these gains to complementary evidence and test-time exploration.

items.title: Pre-Crime for Agents, at the Last Second: Probing When a Recruited Agent Gives In
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40588v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When AI agents share channels and credentials, one agent can press another to break its operator's rule, a first step towards collusion. Output filters check only what an agent has already written. Can an overseer tell beforehand that an agent is about to give in? We show that a linear probe on the agent's activations can, in a controlled multi-agent setting. Across six scenarios, a peer presses a target for up to 20 rounds to reveal a secret, such as a deploy token; the target often refuses, then gives in. Read at each model call before its output is written, the probe picks out the one that leaks. On held-out Qwen3-32B episodes, at a threshold set to flag 5% of benign calls, it catches 82% of leaking calls. At a similar flag rate, a zero-shot decision-model monitor catches 26%. On gpt-oss-20b, a probe on its reasoning reaches AUROC 0.91. A bag-of-words classifier trained on the same calls comes close, so most of the gain comes from training on labels, not activations. The probe also flags permitted disclosures: it reads the coming disclosure more than the violation. The warning is short-range, and halting on any alarm would stop most benign episodes, which a second text check does not fix. A warning raised before generation could let an overseer stop an agent that is about to give in, ahead of others acting on its messages or recruitment spreading through a swarm.

items.title: Collaborative AI agents for autonomous experimental research with solid-state quantum spins
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40589v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An autonomous research laboratory could conduct an entire study, from formulating questions to preparing manuscripts. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers one route towards this goal. Recent AI systems take on several research roles, but may draw conclusions that the evidence does not support. Here, we present an autonomous research laboratory in which agents based on large language models assess one another's work and can stop or redirect investigations. They can generate and reject research questions, require separate theoretical checks and conduct experiments designed to challenge their claims. We demonstrate these capabilities by investigating ensembles of quantum spins in diamond. The agents derived the minimum number of calibration settings needed to predict responses to a defined family of microwave pulse sequences. They checked the result computationally and designed experiments to distinguish competing predictions. An initial experiment agreed with the theoretical predictions, but repeated reference measurements showed that the signal was drifting during data collection. The agents therefore treated the result as inconclusive and revised the measurement protocol without relaxing the acceptance criteria. The revised experiment met those criteria and supported the theoretical predictions. This study demonstrates that collaborating AI agents can select research questions, derive theoretical results and test their predictions experimentally.

items.title: When to Assist and What to Suggest: Joint Gating and Memory-Grounded Hint Generation in One Compact Decoder
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40611v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proactive assistants offer short, memory-grounded hints during a conversation, deciding when to assist and what to suggest. Current systems split this between a gate and a larger generator; we evaluate both together on 28,058 decision points. Stage-wise generation scores are oracle-gate ceilings: behind a real gate, end-to-end exact match is 0.2619 against a ceiling of 0.2971, and end-to-end precision is 0.2387, leaving substantial headroom. A gate pays off through precision and compute, whose saving falls from 4.39x with an 8B generator to 1.38x with a 1B one. The memory profile drives hint quality: removing it costs 24.7 exact-match points (rescaled BERTScore 0.57 to 0.35), while retrieval and a larger generator add nothing on exact match. One 1B decoder can do both, gating from an intermediate layer and generating in the same pass. At its final checkpoint it matches or exceeds the two-model pipelines on automatic end-to-end measures with 1.31-1.76x less wall-clock time than the matched 1B pipeline; across three seeds, its deeper exit ties the separate gate. A human evaluation (1,144 ratings over 32 dialogues) supports the memory effect and rates the single model level with the matched 1B pipeline and below the 8B one. Graded metrics and LlamaPIE's native judge track human ratings more closely than exact match, which we report as a strict lower bound.

items.title: An ODE-based Sampler for Discrete Diffusion Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40618v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The marginals of a continuous diffusion model can be reproduced by a deterministic ordinary differential equation (ODE), known as the probability flow ODE, which provides a foundation for accelerated sampling and consistency distillation. In this paper we address the question whether an analogous formulation exists for discrete diffusion models and answer it affirmatively by introducing exponential residual flows (ERFs). Our framework augments the discrete state with a continuous residual variable for each token and position. These residuals evolve deterministically according to piecewise-defined ODEs whose vector fields depend on the current discrete state and the forward and backward rate matrices of the prescribed diffusion model. The discrete state changes whenever a residual reaches zero. We prove that this construction preserves the marginals of the original diffusion. We derive a practical discretization of our sampler and specialize it to masked and uniform diffusion. The deterministic trajectories of ERFs support consistency distillation and yield empirical improvements over previous approaches across a variety of benchmarks including code and text generation tasks.

items.title: Testimony from Timelines: Evidence-Grounded Significance Testing of Temporal Clinical Hypotheses
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40619v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ask a language model whether sales tend to dip after a product recall, or whether one side effect tends to follow another after a vaccine, and it answers in a fluent sentence that reads like a finding, with no test behind it. Assertions about how events unfold across many cases fill the Web, and each is a temporal hypothesis that only a significance test over the right records can settle. The verifier must specify the null, select the test and decide which records bear on the hypothesis, and any of these choices can go wrong while the conclusion still comes out right. Yet benchmarks for language-model data analysis grade only the conclusion, with the relevant data handed over. We study the problem in health, where a wrong verdict is costly, and present STRATA, a benchmark that grades every decision on the way to a verdict: 8,735 hypotheses over the clinical timelines of vaccine adverse-event reports, with gold plans, evidence sets, p-values and verdicts derived under a released codebook and reproduced by a deterministic oracle. We also propose ART (articulate, retrieve, test), a staged paradigm that exposes each decision as an inspectable output. Extensive experiments with five model configurations show that systems fail mostly at choosing which records count, a verdict-evidence gap that accuracy alone conceals. ART closes most of this gap and brings a 31B open model to within 0.01 of the frontier models under the same paradigm; the frontier models succeed once given the codebook.

items.title: ShallowDefend: Harnessing Shallow Safety Alignment for Multi-Turn Defender
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40627v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety alignment has enabled large language models to reliably refuse harmful requests directly, yet the same request distributed across a multi-turn conversation still succeeds far too often. This brittleness has a mechanistic root: Alignment is shallow, with safety behavior concentrated in a model's first few output tokens, and existing defenses inherit the weakness, supervising the surface form of the response without ever giving the model an explicit safety decision to learn. We take the opposite view of shallowness: if a short span determines the trajectory of an entire response, that span is the highest-leverage place to intervene, and the defender can occupy it first. We propose Assess $\to$ Decide $\to$ Respond, a framework in which the defender assesses the user's intent, commits to an explicit, parseable safety decision, and only then generates a reply conditioned on it, with the commitment trained by reinforcement learning at the payload turn. Because the decision is a token span, the reward can be a rule: a self-verified reward checks the committed label against the conversation's known nature, requiring no judge and no annotation, while the same format also supports an LLM-as-judge reward over a graded decision space with safe redirection. Across two model families and fourteen benchmarks spanning safety, utility, and helpfulness, our defenders achieve the strongest multi-turn safety in a controlled comparison, maintaining their lead in safety while preserving utility at a modest cost to helpfulness. A per-token KL analysis and interventional probes confirm why this works: training concentrates its effect on the brief deliberation that sets a response's trajectory, and the decision committed there is a causal control point. The very shallowness attackers exploit becomes the mechanism of defense.

items.title: world2vec: Mechanistic world models through latent dynamics learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40637v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: World models can achieve strong control performance without faithfully capturing the dynamics of their environment, limiting their potential for mechanistic interpretability and scientific discovery. Here, we introduce world2vec to learn mechanistic world models without reward information directly from observations and actions. World2vec learns latent dynamics that faithfully reproduce the true system over long prediction horizons, with at least one order of magnitude fewer parameters than DreamerV3, TD-MPC2 and LeWM. This enables state of the art performance in controlling continuous environments from pixels and accurate system identification across a benchmark of 71 attractors, demonstrating how world models are amenable to scientific discovery.

items.title: Rethinking Neural Thickets Without Weight Perturbations
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Neural Thickets hypothesis posits that pretrained language models lie in dense neighborhoods of task-specific experts in weight space, which random Gaussian perturbations can uncover. We reproduce the reported gains, but show that they do not require this geometric explanation. Perturbing a single decoder block already recovers much of the improvement, while keeping the model entirely frozen and adding a random bias to its output logits matches or exceeds full-weight perturbations on most reasoning tasks. This suggests an alternative explanation based on output diversity, validation-based selection, and voting. We formalize this view as Perturb-Select-Vote (PSV), a general procedure that generates perturbed predictors, selects high-performing members on a small validation set, and aggregates their predictions. This interpretation connects Neural Thickets to established inference-time methods, including sampling, self-consistency, and verifier-guided selection. A first-order analysis further shows that small weight perturbations act primarily through their induced logit shifts. We extend this analysis to vision, where logit PSV substantially improves performance under domain shift, including on Earth observation, while full-weight perturbations provide little additional benefit. Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision.

Together, these results suggest that the gains attributed to nearby weight-space experts can instead be obtained through output diversity, selection, and voting. Logit PSV realizes these benefits with a fully frozen model, providing a simple, training-free alternative to full-weight perturbation ensembles across language and vision.

items.title: Propose-Filter-Release: Scaling Noise to Typical Sensitivity via Private Filtering
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40654v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An estimator can be accurate and stable on typical data, yet sensitive to a few possible records. Differentially private mechanisms commonly scale their noise to the worst-case influence of a single record, which lets these records dictate the noise even when the remaining data would allow far less. Removing them first would restore the smaller scale, but the removal must itself be private. We introduce \emph{propose-filter-release} (PFR), which, by privately filtering its input, turns a mechanism that protects the addition or removal of a typical record, one that fits the remaining data, into one that is differentially private in the standard sense, on every input. Using our novel filtering step, PFR requires only a concave friendliness score, which measures how well a record fits a dataset, and a release mechanism that is friendly-DP, that is, private when the changed record fits the remaining data. For every such score and release mechanism, it guarantees differential privacy under public conditions on the number of records, so it is a general privacy primitive, comparable to propose-test-release, and FriendlyCore can be viewed as one of its implementations. We illustrate the generality of PFR by instantiating it for scalar statistics, principal subspace estimation, the KL divergence of user histograms, the effective resistances of a graph, and treatment-rule selection.

items.title: Elucidating the Design Space of LM Data Attribution
items.summary: arXiv:2610.40655v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data attribution methods for Language Models (LMs) are typically evaluated using downstream tasks like fact retrieval. However, existing evaluations vary multiple dataset properties simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate exactly why an attribution algorithm fails. To diagnose these failures, we explore the design space of LLM data attribution, with a primary focus on evaluation. We introduce the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT) for fact tracing, in which we fine-tune LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge, providing unambiguous ground truth for attribution. This synthetic setup allows us to systematically alter one dataset configuration at a time, such as document redundancy and lexical distractors. With this configurable evaluation, we demonstrate that redundancy and distractors consistently degrade attribution performance. Rather than proposing a new estimator, we examine two design choices that are underexplored: the loss used to compute gradients and how per-token attribution scores are aggregated into a document score. We find that the true causal evidence within a training document is highly localized, but standard methods dilute this evidence into noise by averaging attribution scores across the entire document. We find that replacing standard cross-entropy loss gradients with the negative log-odds gradients surfaces the critical tokens from other uninformative ones. We can then aggregate only the top token scores to improve ground truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines on our diagnostic benchmark. The negative log-odds correction also generalizes to FTRACE-TREX, improving counterfactual retraining performance for every method we test, by up to 4.9x.

items.title: LLM-Integrated Bayesian State Space Models for Multimodal Time-Series Forecasting
items.summary: arXiv:2510.20952v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Forecasting in the real world requires integrating structured time-series data with unstructured textual information, but existing methods are architecturally limited by fixed input/output horizons and are unable to model or quantify uncertainty. We address this challenge by introducing LLM-integrated Bayesian State space models (LBS), a novel probabilistic framework for multimodal temporal forecasting. At a high level, LBS consists of two components: (1) a state space model (SSM) backbone that captures the temporal dynamics of latent states from which both numerical and textual observations are generated and (2) a pretrained large language model (LLM) that is adapted to encode textual inputs for posterior state estimation and decode textual forecasts consistent with the latent trajectory. This design enables flexible lookback and forecast windows, principled uncertainty quantification, and improved temporal generalization thanks to the well-suited inductive bias of SSMs toward modeling dynamical systems. Experiments on the TextTimeCorpus benchmark demonstrate that LBS improves the previous state-of-the-art by 13.20% while providing human-readable summaries of each forecast. Our work is the first to unify LLMs and SSMs for joint numerical and textual prediction, offering a novel foundation for multimodal temporal reasoning.

items.title: Accelerated Dataflow: scaling inference in streaming data analytics with efficiency
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22731v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Streaming data analytics helps businesses identify opportunities and spot risks in a timely fashion. As large language model (LLM) usage grows, people are exploring incorporating agents or LLMs in streaming data pipelines to help find patterns in datasets without supervision or interpret natural languages for content moderation. However, most streaming systems are currently optimized for data movement and perform poorly on GPU intensive workloads such as performing inference with LLMs. We introduce a system on Google Cloud Dataflow designed to tackle hybrid streaming machine learning workloads with co-designed autoscaling on heterogeneous worker pools and prefix-aware batching. This increases throughput 1.5x to 2x for streaming pipelines using LLMs while maintaining similar latency with up to 75% peak resource savings and 84% lower peak tail latency compared with existing streaming data processing systems.

items.title: Where Planning Changes the Outcome of Orbital Games
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37686v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper introduces OrbitalGym, a simulation environment for studying when planning algorithms or system design determine the outcome of adversarial orbital encounters. In an orbital game, two non-cooperative teams of satellites maneuver during rendezvous and proximity operations to win a differential-reward objective. Advances in terrestrial game playing have prompted many methods for orbital games, but studies typically evaluate one method in one scenario, often against a passive or random defender. It is unclear whether better planning matters once vehicle capability (maneuverability, sensing, communications) and adversarial responses are considered. OrbitalGym is a JAX-based environment supporting varying numbers of agents, state representations (position, velocity, attitude, fuel), explicit or implicit communication, and proximity or conical field-of-view sensors. It compiles games to batched GPU code, enabling large-scale parallel simulation of policies across many configurations. This identifies regimes where policy choice affects outcomes and regimes where system capability dominates. We study two close-range games: pursuit-evasion, where one spacecraft tries to capture another, and lady-bandit-guard, where a guard prevents an attacker from reaching a protected asset. We compare PD, LQR, model predictive path integral control, and Monte Carlo tree search over ratios of thrust and propellant, initial separation, game duration, sensor capability, and the definition of capture. In pursuit-evasion the propellant ratio decides most encounters: against five of six evader policies, pursuer policy changes capture probability by 10 percent or more in at most 15 of 90 capability configurations. In lady-bandit-guard, policy matters more: against bandits able to reach the asset, a better guard policy raises defense probability by at least 10 percent in 56 to 74 of 90 configurations.

items.title: GenAI as an 'Invisible Hand' in Opinion Dynamics: Evidence from a Group-Level Simulation Study
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37689v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent arguments suggest that genAI can act as an invisible hand that gradually shapes social structures, such as collective beliefs and norms. The argument is that if millions of people repeatedly consult genAI tools, their generated outcomes quietly shape what becomes acceptable, reasonable or conventional. We study this in the context of collective opinion dynamics, i.e., how groups form opinions around controversial dynamics. We present the findings of a simulation including 50,000 group discussions across 50 controversial statements, three LLMs, and different social configurations. We vary two characteristics of LLM interaction-agreeableness and personalization-and compare the influence of genAI in homogeneous and heterogeneous groups. Our findings indicate that profile-specific personalization increases LLM influence when models adopt a non-neutral stance, i.e., when they agree or disagree with the user. Furthermore, we find that neutral LLMs have a stronger effect in homogeneous groups. Based on our simulation, we generate a set of hypotheses to specify how, why and when AI-related features and social configurations jointly shape collective opinion making.

items.title: Cassette-Editor: A Video Editing Agent That Edits the Way You Do
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37690v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language agents increasingly work by calling tools on a persistent artifact, such as a code repository, and the result of each call shapes their next step. Video editing is a demanding case of this pattern: what a frame shows depends on how every clip is trimmed, retimed, cropped, and nested, so knowledge about the footage holds only for particular uses of it, and an invalid edit can leave the timeline structurally broken. Existing video editing agents keep their edits valid with critic agents, reviewers, or restricted output formats. We present Cassette-Editor, a video editing agent with a deliberately simple interface: one tool reads the project and one tool writes to it. Every write passes through the same executor, rules, and commit service as the user's manual edits, and either commits atomically or is rejected with located diagnostics and repair options, while the model keeps the creative choices and decides how to recover. Reads relate stored analysis of the footage to each use of it on the timeline. In a controlled experiment, a real model is shown 277 of its own committed edits after damaging them. It corrected nearly every call with full or minimal feedback, but locating each problem cut the input tokens a correction needed to less than half, and its corrections dropped other values the model had written in one case rather than seven.

items.title: Two-Colour Zig-Zag Numberlink on Rectangles: A Forbidden-Pattern Characterization, a Constructive Polynomial-Time Algorithm, and a Lean Verification
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37691v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In Zig-Zag Numberlink, pairs of endpoints in a grid must be joined by vertex-disjoint paths that together visit every cell. The problem is NP-complete when the number of pairs is un- bounded (Adcock et al.). For a single pair it is the Hamiltonian path problem in rectangular grid graphs, solved by Itai, Papadimitriou and Szwarcfiter. Two pairs on a rectangle form the paired 2-disjoint path cover problem. We settle the case of two pairs on rectangles with the endpoints anywhere in the grid. If both sides of the rectangle are at least 11, an instance is solvable if and only if no entry of a finite catalogue of forbidden patterns occurs. The catalogue consists of a parity condition, an alternation condition on the border, a handful of local corner and edge patterns, 65 listed corner configurations, and a rule that propagates forced routes out of the corners before testing alternation. If a side is at most 10, a frontier dynamic programming algorithm decides the instance in time linear in the long side. The characterization is construc- tive. Solutions are built by deleting empty lines, splitting the rectangle by straight cuts, and splicing the pieces back together, in time O((R+C) RC). Both directions of the characterization and the correctness of the dynamic programming algorithm are verified in Lean 4. The finite case analyses, which are window certificates for the corner configurations and a check of all irreducible instances with sides 11-22, are carried out by the Lean compiler via native decide. We describe the algorithm, the catalogue, the proof structure, the compromises made in the formalization, and implementations in Python, JavaScript and C that produce identical output.

items.title: Network Topology Does Not Matter: The Breakdown of Classical Consensus in LLM Populations
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37699v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: As multi-agent language model networks become widely deployed, predicting their collective behavior is a critical challenge. Classical distributed consensus theory relies on network topology to predict convergence, structurally assuming that agent updates are convex combinations, population means are conserved, and weights are content-independent. In this work, we demonstrate that these foundational assumptions fail for large language models (LLMs). By deterministically extracting continuous credence from token-level probabilities across eight instruction-tuned models and 73,080 controlled exchanges, we directly measure the empirical LLM update operator. We find that LLMs systematically violate convexity by updating outside the hull of observed opinions, exhibiting active repulsion (negative weights) that fundamentally breaks row-stochastic modeling and standard bounded-confidence repairs. Scaling these empirically fitted operators to simulations of 10,000 agents reveals that algebraic connectivity explains almost none of the final outcome variance. Instead, population dynamics are governed entirely by the model's internal update bias and message framing. Consequently, populations of several models, including those with up to 7B parameters, reliably compound small local drifts to reach confident agreement on objectively false claims regardless of their network structure. Our results prove that classical graph-theoretic metrics are inadequate for LLM populations, highlighting a profound deployment risk where multi-agent deliberation predictably saturates in collective delusion.

items.title: The Coordination Tax and the Heterogeneity Dividend: Break-Even Conditions for Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37700v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent LLM pipelines built on interoperability protocols such as the Open Floor Protocol (OFP) or A2A are usually justified on capability grounds, with their runtime cost treated as an overhead of unknown size. Comparing such a pipeline with one model call is underspecified, because a pipeline can give each role a different model. We give a closed-form model that sets the coordination tax (decomposition overhead plus per-handoff protocol cost) against the heterogeneity dividend from routing work to a cheaper model, with a break-even threshold and a feasibility bound, $\alpha < 1/r$, and measure every term, with OFP as the protocol under test, on 135 HumanEval and ClassEval tasks in 2430 runs of six architectures with Claude Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. The protocol adds 7.2 ms per handoff, 0.11% of pipeline wall time. Decomposition does not pay on these tasks: a planner-coder-reviewer pipeline costs 3.22x as much as a single strong call, takes 3.24x as long, and solves no more tasks. Moving planner and reviewer to the cheap model cuts the pipeline's cost to 0.39x but changes pass@1 by -6.7 points, leaving it dearer, slower and less accurate than the single call, and the break-even forecast misses by -19% because the cheap roles inflate token volume. The saving lies in choosing a model per task instead: an oracle choice between the two single calls solves 94.3% of runs at half the strong call's cost per solved task.

items.title: DuQUAD: A Dual-View Framework with Quality-Aware Evidence Pruning for Multi-Document Question Answering
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37701v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models with retrieval-augmented generation systematically underutilize evidence in the middle of multi-document contexts, a phenomenon known as Lost in the Middle. Existing mitigation strategies, such as document reordering and attention steering, can reduce boundary bias but remain brittle in noisy settings, where inaccurate relevance estimation and spurious documents still obscure useful evidence in central positions. We propose DuQUAD, a multi-document QA framework that mitigates positional bias through dual-view reasoning and quality-aware evidence pruning. DuQUAD combines a Local Agent guided by a Structural Fusion Score with a Global Agent that reasons over the full document set, providing both targeted evidence recovery and broad contextual understanding. The framework further filters candidate evidence using explicit quality scoring and refines it at the sentence level to reduce noise. DuQUAD consistently outperforms strong Lost-in-the-Middle mitigation baselines, including hybrid retrieval and reranking, multi-agent reasoning, and context optimization methods, improving accuracy by 3.0% on average over the strongest competing baseline and gold evidence recall by 9.4%, while substantially reducing computational cost compared to existing multi-agent frameworks.

items.title: Search-Guided Reasoning Trace Curation for Verilog Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37706v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have improved Verilog generation. However, most training pipelines distill natural-language reasoning traces whose intermediate design decisions are weakly structured and are primarily selected according to the correctness of the final generated RTL. We present MCTS-SFT, a verifier-guided framework for curating reasoning traces for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of Verilog generation models. MCTS-SFT formulates trace construction as search over intermediate reasoning states and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to propagate functional feedback from complete Verilog rollouts to earlier design decisions. Within this framework, we introduce Plan-MCTS, which searches over compact hardware-design plans that explicitly represent interfaces, timing, state, behavior, and update rules. We further study plan-preserving supervision, in which the searched structured state is retained as part of the downstream SFT target. Our experiments find that Plan-MCTS achieves the highest functional trace yield, with 84.2% correct traces compared with 81.9% for one-shot structured planning and 82.0% for unguided tree exploration. For identical Plan-MCTS trajectories and Verilog outputs, retaining the explicit searched plan during SFT raises pass@10 from 52.56% to 57.7%, demonstrating that the representation of intermediate design decisions materially affects downstream learning. In a separate 6,000-trace study, MCTS-curated supervision improves pass@10 over full-response chain-of-thought distillation by up to 3.7 points while reducing downstream generation length by approximately 50% on VerilogEval-v2. These results demonstrate that structured hardware planning, verifier-guided search, and explicit intermediate-state supervision provide complementary mechanisms for constructing more effective and token-efficient training data for Verilog generation.

MCTS-SFT formulates trace construction as search over intermediate reasoning states and uses Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to propagate functional feedback from complete Verilog rollouts to earlier design decisions. Within this framework, we introduce Plan-MCTS, which searches over compact hardware-design plans that explicitly represent interfaces, timing, state, behavior, and update rules. We further study plan-preserving supervision, in which the searched structured state is retained as part of the downstream SFT target. Our experiments find that Plan-MCTS achieves the highest functional trace yield, with 84.2% correct traces compared with 81.9% for one-shot structured planning and 82.0% for unguided tree exploration. For identical Plan-MCTS trajectories and Verilog outputs, retaining the explicit searched plan during SFT raises pass@10 from 52.56% to 57.7%, demonstrating that the representation of intermediate design decisions materially affects downstream learning. In a separate 6,000-trace study, MCTS-curated supervision improves pass@10 over full-response chain-of-thought distillation by up to 3.7 points while reducing downstream generation length by approximately 50% on VerilogEval-v2. These results demonstrate that structured hardware planning, verifier-guided search, and explicit intermediate-state supervision provide complementary mechanisms for constructing more effective and token-efficient training data for Verilog generation.

items.title: Relevance-Guided Residual Calibration for Spectral Compression of Dense Retrieval Embeddings
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37707v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spectral compression reduces the storage and scoring costs of dense retrieval by projecting embeddings onto a smaller principal subspace. However, its corpus-derived weighting rules tie all retained directions to a shared spectral trend, without directly accounting for their individual contributions to relevance. To address this, we propose Relevance-Guided Residual Calibration (RRC), a closed-form method for refining spectral weights using relevance judgments. RRC estimates margin-based weights from the means and variances of positive--negative score contributions along each retained direction. It retains directions with positive estimated weights, decomposes their log weights into a fitted power-law trend and a residual, and adds the residual to the compressor's log weights on this support. This allows relevance judgments to adjust individual directions while preserving the compressor's overall spectral trend. RRC applies to PCA, Whitening, and SpecTemp, and incorporates the corrections into the existing transformation shared by documents and queries, without iterative model training or an additional inference stage. Experiments with three encoders on nine datasets covering conventional and reasoning-intensive retrieval show that SpecTemp + RRC achieves the highest mean effectiveness among tested compressors on the BEIR group and BRIGHT at every target dimension. On the five evaluated BRIGHT datasets, it improves over SpecTemp by an average of 2.34 nDCG@10 points at 768 dimensions. The gains also persist under scalar and product quantization, improving the trade-off between per-document storage and retrieval effectiveness. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/rrc-spectral-compression-B5CE/

items.title: Towards Myocardial Infarction Diagnosis: An Investigation into Machine Learning and Deep Learning Algorithms using ECG Data
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37709v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Myocardial Infarction (MI) is a severe and potentially fatal cardiac condition caused by myocardial injury due to ischemia, and timely detection can substantially reduce its mortality. Electrocardiography (ECG) is the primary diagnostic modality for MI, but manual interpretation is susceptible to human error. In this work, we propose Visionary V2, a multi-step, adaptive filtration method for ECG signal normalization, and use it to study machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches to MI detection on the PTB Diagnostic ECG Database using all 15 available leads. On statistical features extracted from the filtered signals, such as the R-R interval, a Bagging ensemble of decision trees reaches 96.6% accuracy, compared with 87.7% when the signals are processed with BioSPPy. We further generate an image dataset from the filtered signals, on which a custom ResNet-50 misclassifies only 1 of 7,000 validation images and a custom CNN reaches an F1 score of about 98.7%. Finally, we apply LIME, Grad-CAM and Integrated Gradients to verify that the image models attend to the ECG waveform rather than the background. These results indicate that careful signal normalization combined with ML and DL models can support fast and accurate automated MI screening.

items.title: Generation, Not Selection: LLM Proposals for Certified Access-Control Policy Mining
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37716v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) policy mining---recovering a compact, auditable policy from an access log---is posed as minimum set cover and solved greedily, which enjoys an $s^{*}(1+\ln m)$ guarantee. That guarantee is \emph{conditional} on a precondition the literature never states: the candidate pool handed to greedy must contain the optimal rules. Generation, not selection, is the binding constraint, and existing generators are purely \emph{syntactic}---they surface a rule only when enough log records witness it, so they fail on precisely the rare exception rules that fill a heavy-tailed policy. We replace the generator with a language model proposing rules \emph{semantically}, from attribute names, and keep the combinatorial selector to carry the guarantee: every proposal is filtered against the observed denials, so soundness is independent of the proposal mechanism and an unreliable proposer can only waste candidates, never grant access. Over five seeds on each of two enterprise domains, adding semantic proposal to a syntactic miner dominates it on \emph{ten of ten} runs---strictly better on seven---with near-optimal policies ($9.2$--$9.6$ rules against $s^{*}=9$, versus $11.2$--$14.6$) and false grants cut four- to sevenfold. Replacing the syntactic miner rather than augmenting it wins only where witnesses are scarce. An anonymization ablation isolates the mechanism: opaque attribute names cost two thirds of the model's rule recovery while leaving the syntactic baselines provably unmoved, and cost nothing where witnesses are plentiful. Semantic knowledge and log evidence are substitutes.

items.title: Learning Graph Beliefs for Active Radio Mapping With Decision-Certified Multi-Step Sensing
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37717v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Radio maps provide essential wireless propagation knowledge for network optimization and autonomous platforms. Acquiring dense measurements, however, is prohibitively costly, requiring active sampling to prioritize informative measurements. Existing active sampling methods typically rely on variances from prescribed spatial models or learned pointwise uncertainty, which may not fully capture the spatial correlation of different measurements. This paper proposes GraphBARC, a graph-structured active radio map construction framework that integrates learned spatial modeling with analytical Bayesian inference. A graph network learns correlated node and edge factors using only acquired measurements, inducing a joint full-map belief that supports analytical observation updates without retraining. Rather than immediate one-step acquisition, it adopts a nonmyopic sensing strategy that evaluates joint map-wide Bayes risk reduction over feasible multi-step routes, accounting for information redundancy among planned measurements. We reuse candidate responses and derive residual-based bounds directly on route-value differences, retaining shared response-error structure to avoid uniformly high-accuracy evaluation. An error-aware continuation bound screens unpromising prefixes, after which only responses needed for unresolved comparisons are refined. We further establish a computable decision-gap bound and show that certified exclusions remain valid during refinement. Experiments show that GraphBARC reduces mean root-mean-square error (RMSE) by over 16% relative to the evaluated baselines and core planning time by 56% compared with the fixed-accuracy, unpruned implementation.

items.title: FVH-Bench: Evaluating Image Generator Safety Beyond Overtly Harmful Imagery
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37722v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern image generators can produce complex visual artifacts, including diagrams, interfaces, and records that combine text, graphics, and layout to convey detailed information. They may refuse requests for overtly harmful imagery yet still generate artifacts that guide dangerous actions or support deception. We call the risk arising from what such images enable, rather than only what they depict, functional visual harm (FVH). Existing safety benchmarks focus largely on overtly harmful content, such as pornography and graphic violence, leaving image generators' safety alignment against FVH insufficiently evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce FVH-Bench, comprising 669 prompts across five harmful visual functions and ten risk domains. The 11 evaluated image generators rarely refuse these requests and frequently generate artifacts that fulfill the targeted harmful functions. High scores for target harm realization and harmful artifact usability further indicate that these outputs can support the intended harmful purposes. A further analysis finds that existing safety detectors also provide limited coverage of FVH, indicating gaps in their ability to recognize harmful visual functions. Together, these findings show that evaluating image-generator safety alignment requires considering not only what images depict, but also what they may enable.

items.title: Beyond Similarity Search: Knowledge Graph Metadata Enrichment for Enterprise Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37728v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A key challenge of RAG systems is retrieving information from enterprise documents created by multiple teams over time, where it is not possible to enrich the information using the latest information and metadata available outside the scope of organizational documentation responsibility. We investigated whether using a knowledge graph to store metadata and frequently changing information would improve upon knowledge retrieval over similarity search over embeddings. To perform the experiment, we created a snapshot of the SEC EDGAR dataset for a quarter, comprising 167,050 filings from 10,511 companies and 508,714 embedded chunks of risk-factor text. To simulate the enrichment, we created a knowledge graph of 430,257 nodes and 561,144 edges carrying an accession number on every edge. To evaluate the gain obtained via a graph-based design, we evaluated three architectures: text-to-SQL over typed columns, dense-vector RAG with HNSW cosine search, and a two-stage GraphRAG design. All architectures share the same model and temperature to allow comparison. Results are scored programmatically by an LLM as judge over 20 questions divided across four categories, each question asked three times. GraphRAG solved 16 of 20 questions on all three attempts, compared to 10 for text-to-SQL and 3 for vector RAG. GraphRAG lost on structured aggregation queries. Vector RAG lost the single-document category it was expected to win, passing 3 of 15 where GraphRAG passed 15 of 15, because company attribution is not recoverable from cosine similarity at this scale. All six confident falsehoods in the benchmark were text-to-SQL conflating distinct people who share a surname, the failure that resolving identity to an identifier before reading any text prevents structurally; GraphRAG made none. We claim no advantage beyond this corpus, this model and this question set.

items.title: When Skills Tell Agents Not to Ask: A Large-Scale Study of Oversight Directives in Agent Skills
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37734v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Agent skills, reusable instruction packages centred on a SKILL.md file, extend AI agents on demand, and a single line in a widely copied skill reaches every agent that loads it. Some lines are oversight-loosening directives: they tell the agent to proceed without approval, to bypass checks with --no-verify, or to keep working without checking in. Although such directives can remove a checkpoint from every agent that loads them, no prior work has examined them. We present the first large-scale study of oversight-loosening directives, analyzing 1.53 million English skills from GitSkills. We split skills into units (sentences, bullets, table cells, and code lines), develop a codebook that labels oversight directives by polarity, mechanism, and scope, label 2,097 units by hand, and train a detector to scale the analysis. Our results show that about one in seventeen skills (about 88,000 skills) contains a loosening directive. These directives most often loosen oversight through permission flags, and most of them (70.1%) apply unconditionally rather than only in specific contexts such as CI. Compared with skills that have the same amount of oversight language, skills that run shell code, install packages, or use sudo have 1.7-1.8 times the odds of containing a loosening directive, an association that holds across all our robustness checks, and they do not compensate with more tightening. Loosening spreads through a few upstream skills rather than through edits by their adopters: 2.4% of the skill families that carry loosening account for half of all copies of loosening-carrying skills, and 1.1% of distinct loosening units for half of all loosening occurrences. Open-source skill scanners catch at most 46% of loosening directives, with a precision below 0.4, while the LLM behind them, prompted with our codebook instead, catches 61% at a precision of 0.71.

items.title: Poisoned Skills: Propagating Jailbreaks Through Agent Markdown Files
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37738v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern agent frameworks allow users to provide Markdown files containing system prompts, tool descriptions, and skill definitions (e.g., SKILL.md), which are incorporated into the agent's context during initialization. In this work, we investigate whether this configuration mechanism can also serve as an injection channel: can a jailbreak embedded in a Markdown skill file propagate through an agent and induce prohibited behavior? To answer this question, we construct a LangChain-based question-answering agent whose system prompt is assembled from a user-provided Markdown file. We embed a jailbreak combining persona manipulation with a GPTFUZZER-based attack and evaluate its effectiveness across seven contemporary open-weight models using 270 forbidden questions spanning nine harm categories. Under a benign system prompt, the models exhibit near-complete refusal behavior, with a mean attack success rate (ASR) of just 0.5%. In contrast, the injected skill file raises the mean ASR to 45%, reaching 68.9% for individual models. We further evaluate two payload obfuscation strategies: an invisible zero-width character-based stealth payload and a phonetic payload based on grapheme-to-phoneme transformations. Neither outperforms the plain-text injection; notably, the phonetic variant reduces mean ASR to 30%. These findings identify Markdown skill files as an underexplored attack surface for AI agents and suggest that vulnerability to configuration-based jailbreaks depends more strongly on the underlying model than on the specific payload obfuscation technique.

items.title: EUReCA: End-to-End Unified CBCT Reconstruction Across Clinical Acquisitions
items.summary: arXiv:2610.37740v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is widely used for image-guided radiotherapy, but reducing the number of projections to lower dose and scan time makes reconstruction increasingly ill-posed. We present EUReCA (End-to-end Unified REconstruction across Clinical Acquisitions), a geometry-aware feed-forward model for variable-view clinical linac CBCT. For a given acquisition trajectory, EUReCA accepts 8-100 projections with a single set of weights, without view-count-specific retraining; the same architecture and training recipe extend unchanged to other clinical trajectories. It combines learned projection features with an in-frame Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstruction. The model encodes each projection with a shared multiscale backbone, back-projects features into multiresolution 3D grids using the acquisition geometry, aggregates variable numbers of views at fixed computational cost, and refines the volume with a global 3D transformer and multilevel decoder. On simulated data, EUReCA achieved 29.9-33.2 dB PSNR with 10-100 views and outperformed all applicable feed-forward baselines; it also exceeded iterative optimization-based methods while running orders of magnitude faster. On 15 measured patient CBCT scans evaluated against vendor reconstructions, EUReCA achieved the best performance at every tested view count. These results suggest that geometry-aware, measurement-anchored feed-forward reconstruction can provide a practical and flexible foundation for variable-view linac CBCT.
